Previously, we have discussed how there is little other safe bonds to buy. Last year’s 10y foreign takedown data seem to support that view as well (Figure 7). Typically, foreign takedown at 10y auctions is persistent. And the strength of the new issue auctions, which are quarterly in Feb/May/Aug/Nov, tends to be a function of foreign takedown. As we show in Figure 8, the recent strength bodes well for foreign takedown at the next auction (tentatively scheduled Feb 11th). Turning to spreads, a Warsh Chair does not have us too concerned on our 5y spreads long. We still like our long, even if the typical bullish pattern in 5y spreads is breaking down slightly to start 2026 (Figure 9). In fact, we think investors should extend out of 2y spreads and into 3y to 5y which we think is the sweet spot. Shifts in SOMA WAM should have little impact on 5y swap spreads. Most funding tail risks are contained with the current reserve backdrop, due to the large RMPs. We also think carry trades make sense with macro in a bit of a holding pattern (we are paid 1y1y SOFR/TONAR for carry in FX Basis Quarterly - Carrying on but with caution). records.text: US Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 9 Core views Growth: a dose of optimism • Our 2026 average US GDP growth forecast of 2.8% is well above consensus (2.1%). The key drivers are easier fiscal and monetary policy, and our expectation of more growth-friendly trade policy. We now project that consumer stimulus from the OBBBA will be more front-loaded into tax season. This prompts us to tweak our forecasts: we modestly raise 1H 2026 growth and lower 2H. Risks to our projections are tilted to the upside. A 3-handle on 2026 growth wouldn’t be a big surprise. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We continue to expect inflation to remain above the Fed's target throughout our forecast horizon. In the near term, supply-driven inflation due to tariffs should push inflation above 3% y/y through 3Q 2026 as businesses continue to slowly shift costs to consumers. Inflationary pressures from tariffs should fade towards the end of 2026; however, core PCE inflation should end 2026 at an elevated 2.9% y/y and only decline to 2.4% by year end 2027. We continue to believe underlying inflation is above 2%, and our growth and monetary policy outlook should generate more demand driven inflation causing a delay in inflation’s return to the Fed’s 2% target. records.text: After cutting in December, the Committee indicated that Bank Rate remains on a downward path but signalled caution around the pace of further easing, suggesting that there is little chance of a second consecutive rate reduction. Moreover, the latest data have been mixed and so are unlikely to change the MPC’s position. The labour market figures continue to look weak, with the unemployment rate remaining at 5.1%, payrolled employment contracting further, and survey indicators of employment growth remaining soft. But there have been signs of firmer growth momentum, with the monthly GDP, retail sales, and flash PMI numbers all surprising to the upside. On the nominal side, wage growth decelerated slightly more than expected and now looks likely to marginally undershoot the Bank’s forecasts for Q4. But headline inflation came in slightly above expectations and sequential measures of underlying services inflation ticked up. T oday’s market reaction is roughly playing out as we write in our Kevin Warsh deep dive (see US Rates Weekly - New Year, New Fed Pick). We see the new Fed Chair nominee as an ardent believer that the Fed’s larger balance sheet distorts market prices. Based on his comments in his November WSJ op-ed, reducing the sheet would allow “That largesse can be redeployed in the form of lower interest rates. ” We reiterated that this announcement would be a bull steepener, combined with some risk of more negative 30y spreads, which are roughly playing out. At the same time, the market is slightly pricing in rate hikes in 2027 /2028, presumably since Kevin Warsh has historically highlighted inflation risks. In our view, that was a very different inflation world and not as relevant today, but we understand the slight increase in risks. What happens on the balance sheet? We think it will be hard for Warsh to restart QT outright given the repo volatility last year (see Alejandra’s short-end notes below). records.text: 29 January 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 11 Figure 9: SPF: Deviation in 5-year ahead expectations from inflation target (pp) Figure 10: Market pricing: Forward swap implied inflation expectations, deviation from inflation target (pp) Source: Deutsche Bank Research, ECB Source: Deutsche Bank Research, Bloomberg Finance LP Degree of anchoring measure Simply looking at average expectations can be misleading. For example, if half the population expects 0% inflation and the other half expects 4%, the average is a perfect 2%. Yet, not a single person actually expects inflation to hit the target, and the wi de disagreement would be a concern for policymakers. To get a clearer picture, we must also look beyond the average and analyse the entire distribution of expectations. Therefore, we extend our analysis of the level criteria to a measure of the degree of anchoring used by Naggert et al (2023) of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. This measure quadratically penalises expectations away from the target. Figure 11: Definition of degree of anchoring measure Source: Deutsche Bank Research We construct this measure for the household inflation expectations using the dbDataInsights survey, and for professionals using the SPF survey results based on the individual responses (Figure 12). records.text: lizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 50k in 2026 after coming in at 15k in 2H25. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate ticking up to just 4.5% in 4Q25, where it should remain in 1H26 before dropping to 4.3% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5-3.75% at the January meeting, as expected. In the characterization of current conditions, the Fed leaned into the Dec u-rate decline. Powell’s comments on the labor market mirrored the optimism in the statement. But he also highlighted some pockets of concern. We remain comfortable with our view that the Fed won’t cut again under Powell. We have penciled in two 25bp cuts under the next Chair, with low conviction, in June and July. Policy under the next Chair will depend a lot on the composition of the FOMC. This leaves our projection of the terminal rate unchanged at 3.0-3.25%.

In that case, the policy trajectory could be adjusted by adding the DPP's economic policies to those of the LDP and Ishin. ECB preview Mounting uncertainty, maximum optionality We expect unchanged ECB policy rates and balance sheet policies, and no major changes to the monetary policy statement. With these considerations in mind, we are making changes to the Japan Equity Focus List. Specifically, we remove Sony Group (6758) and add Fujitsu (6702). As defense policy emphasis expands from equipment itself to domains such as C4ISR (command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance), cyber, and data utilization, we think the scope to reassess Fujitsu’s business positioning is increasing. records.text: f Economist Lane mentioned in a December speech that if people simply extrapolate inflation when forming expectations then “ a persistent shift in the inflation rate can influence the formation of inflation expectations if people put some weight on simple extrapolation in forming expectations. Under such extrapolative behaviour, if inflation runs below target for a year or two, there is some risk that people might revise down their beliefs about the de facto medium-term inflation target”. In the accounts of the December meeting the inflation undershoot was called by one member “a cause for concern ” as it could lead to a downwards unanchoring of inflation expectations. To assess how well anchored inflation expectations are, we have put together a framework to holistically examine inflation expectations in the euro area. The framework is based on criteria for well -anchored inflation expectations outlined by New York Federal Reserve President John Williams in a 2022 speech. According to his thinking, well-anchored expectations satisfy the following three criteria: – Sensitivity – “Although near - and medium -term inflation expectations may respond to economic shocks, expectations of inflation far into the future should not”. records.text: Most Policy Rate Simulations Likely Lower than in November but Forward-Looking Rule Could Imply Marginally Less Easing We now assess how the Bank’s model-based policy simulations could change. To do so, we construct a small macro model that approximates the Bank’s (much larger) structural model. We then follow the Bank’s method of fitting the model to the central projection and finding the paths for Bank Rate, the output gap and inflation under different monetary policy rules or optimal policy. We describe our methodology in more detail in the appendix. Our model generates policy paths broadly similar to those published in the November MPR. Note that these paths are conditional on the Bank’s projections, and would look different under our own economic forecasts. Exhibit 7 shows the paths generated by our model based on our expectation for the updated central projections at the February meeting. The contemporaneous Taylor rule – in which policy responds to current inflation and the output gap – is likely to show a steeper decline in Bank Rate compared with the path shown in November given the lower near-term inflation projection. That said, the magnitude of the change is limited by the fact that the rule places less weight on contributions to inflation from energy. The optimal policy projection, which aims to achieve the best trade-off between output and inflation, should also show more easing than before given lower near-term inflation. 4 US Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 A different kind of overheating The Fed will likely be inertial in coming around to a higher neutral rate. Particularly under the next Chair, who is likely to lean into a low neutral rate view (similar to Governor Miran), as a way of justifying their (expected) dovish leaning. This creates risk of overheating later this year and into 2027. Our above-consensus inflation forecast of 2.8% y/y core PCE at year-end is premised on i) an economy that is running hot due to fiscal and monetary easing, and ii) additional tariff pass-through in coming months. One reason we aren’t expecting a much bigger inflation wave from policy easing is the K-shaped nature of consumer spending. Asset-rich higher-income households are already seeing strong spending growth. Therefore, their marginal propensity to spend any additional income/wealth could be somewhat low at this stage: instead, they might invest in financial markets. Our conclusion is that if if the Fed ends up over-easing, the impact could be felt more in asset inflation than price inflation.

records.text: Ben Luk 29 January 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Emerging Markets Weekly : Reset ting Asia We have pursued a n aggressive risk-on strategy since the start of 2026 with a preference towards EM ex-Asia carry against USD as well as RV opportunities within Asia. While the initial trades worked brilliantly with TRY, ZAR and CLP all gaining, our bets in Asia were mixed especially given the surge in the JPY. Institutional investors remain somewhat cautious towards EM even though DXY is back to a 4 -year low as local currency sovereign bonds and equity flows remain negative while FX flows have recovered. Economic activity: resilient, but external risks cloud the outlook We expect the ECB to judge that economic activity has broadly evolved in line with the December projections, with euro area growth continuing to show resilience despite lingering external headwinds and rising uncertainty. We expect risks to growth to continue to be viewed as two-sided. Hard and soft indicators released since the December macroeconomic projections suggest that the euro area economy likely grew close to trend in Q4. Our nowcasting model points to growth of around 0.3% q/q, implying slight upside risks relative to both our forecast and the ECB's projection of a 0.2% q/q expansion. Survey evidence continues to indicate that growth remains predominantly services-led but the outlook for the manufacturing sector has improved. In November, EA industrial production rose by a robust 0.7% m/m – the third consecutive monthly increase – leaving the carryover for Q4 at 1.0% q/q. records.text: Muted Impact of US Storm on European Balances Winter Storm Fern, which hit the US about a week ago, severely tightened US physical gas balances for a few days by lifting heating-related gas demand at the same time that it disrupted more than 10% of US gas production due to freeze-offs. The resulting spike in day-ahead gas prices incentivized several US liquefaction facilities to sell gas into the grid, instead of using it for liquefaction and exports, resulting in lower LNG cargo loadings from the US in the period. Ultimately, we saw an 11 mtpa (41 mcm/d) decline in US exports on a four-week-moving average basis by January 29th relative to one week prior, implying a similar size drop in global LNG supplies delivered during February. Despite the temporary drop in US exports, we expect NW European LNG imports in February to remain largely unchanged vs our previous expectations, as we expect Europe to take a bigger share of global supply than we expected previously. Specifically, spot Asia LNG prices (JKM) have not fully chased the recent weather-driven rally in TTF, strengthening the incentive for LNG sellers to deliver in Europe vs Asia (Exhibit 2). While we think this lack of strong Asia competition for cargoes is partly due to LNG prices having moved back above oil parity, incentivizing gas-to-oil switching (Exhibit 3), we believe growing nuclear (Japan) and renewable (China) generation are also weighing on Asia’s natural gas demand. But the real policy rate looks to be very close to the Fed’s r* estimate. • Moreover, the Fed appears to be underestimating potential growth (and therefore r*). Policy might already be accommodative. • We see risks of overheating due to easy fiscal and monetary policy in coming months. But in a K-shaped economy, that might be reflected in financial asset inflation rather than price inflation. The neutral rate debate is shifting into higher gear With the economic outlook improving, we think the most important question for the Fed this year will be: where is the neutral rate, and how is it impacted by growing evidence of accelerating labor productivity? This matters because if policy is already neutral, the case to cut rates would hinge mostly on the labor data. Even if inflation were a bit softer than expected, there wouldn’t be a compelling reason to cut if the labor and activity data are steady. But if policy is still restrictive, it could be easier to lower rates on disinflation alone. Chair Powell got a few questions around these issues at the January press conferences. records.text: United States: Treasuries 2025 Treasury auctions: Domestic and foreign demand intact Ahead of the upcoming QRA, we take a look at Treasury auction demand, which remained resilient in 2025. Domestic buyers took down record supply, and foreign participation strengthened into year-end. Despite fiscal and tariff concerns, the auction data show no material signs of weakness This is a reprint of United States: Treasuries: 2025 Treasury auctions: Domestic and foreign demand intact, published on 28 January 2026. Ahead of the upcoming February QRA, where we expect (see here) the Treasury to keep auction sizes of notes/bonds unchanged through the rest of 2026, we review auction demand trends from 2025. In early 2025, concerns around the US fiscal outlook and uncertainty about the administration's tariff agenda led investors to question the demand for US Treasuries. Despite this, demand has held up well at Treasury auctions. When incorporating tariff revenues, fiscal policy under the One Big Beautiful Bill passed last summer is less expansionary than initially feared. Combined with a steady profile for coupon sizes, improved liquidity conditions, and larger long-end buybacks, long-end yields have been contained. Auction demand across investor categories has remained broadly consistent. Concerns that foreign investors would step back from the Treasury market after "Liberation Day" have not materialized—the auction data show little evidence of such behavior. The figures suggest that the LDP is on track to secure a sole majority in the chamber, while the Centrist Reform Alliance looks to lose seats and the Democratic Party for the People would maintain its present standing. Regarding the accuracy of such polls, we recall the bitter experience of the Lower House election in 2021, when most media outlets badly underestimated the number of seats that the LDP would win and thus considerably miscalculated the election results. The polling firms have drawn from this experience and improved their survey methods, boosting their accuracy in subsequent elections. Still, there are many uncertainties this time that make it difficult to rely on past data, such as the transformation in the government framework from the LDP’s long- standing coalition with Komeito to its new alliance with the Japan Innovation Party. The pattern of election cooperation among opposition parties also differs notably from the last election. We believe that such changes could undermine the accuracy of opinion polls. Polls from the final stages of the election campaign, which should be out next week, will be closely watched as a more accurate gauge of voter trends. The changes seen from the early stages will be an important indicator for predicting the late course of the election. ECB – FX back into play President Trump may not be concerned about the dollar slump (see FT, 28Jan26), but the ECB might be. Just before blackout, two members of the GC took the opportunity to speak up on FX. First, there was the ECB’s Kocher telling the FT (28Jan26) that if there was a significant appreciation of the euro that impacted the inflation projections then it could trigger rate cuts. This certainly felt noteworthy coming from the Austrian central bank governor, who traditionally leans hawkish. Then, there was the more centralist GC member Villeroy de Galhau saying the ECB is “closely monitoring” the strength of the euro and what it might mean for inflation (see Bloomberg, 28Jan26). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Self-help – Don't Wait for a Crisis Australian corporates have the potential to chase a new phase of self-help, marked not just by cost discipline but also by a strategic embrace of technology – especially AI – to unlock productivity, resilience and growth. This is more than a late-cycle playbook: it is a structural shift, as firms move early to streamline organizational structures, automate workflows, and tighten working capital and procurement. Recent earnings transcripts and management commentary have shown a pivot from narrative to delivery This season sees the future of work debate being increasingly in focus for investors and policy makers. What seems to be starting as an embracement of labor asset churn and some lag and drag in rehiring intention could turn into more meaningful mix and reskilling focus and, in some cases, outright redundancy of some roles in the most affected industry verticals. Stocks that come up in discussion for self-help potential include: ANZ, AGL, CSL, IAG, MQG, REA, TLS, TLC, TCL and WOW. FX and growth | Strong euro weighs on exports: For growth, the main channel of transmission of exchange rate shocks goes through exports and imports. And here, rather than focusing only on the dollar, we like to think in terms of the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) with a broader group of partners weighted by their significance in euro area external trade in manufactured goods and services. While the euro is up ca 3% against the dollar since November (when the ECB froze assumptions for its Dec projections), it has appreciated by around 1% in nominal effective terms. A ratio of ca 2:1 between the two broad measures of euro strength reflects historical trends (Exhibit 36 ). As for the macro impacts, on our estimates, a 5% appreciation of the euro in effective terms would reduce euro area exports by 1.5%, with an impact of around -0.3pp on euro area GDP. Estimates across countries suggest exports from France, Italy and Spain react more to the euro effective exchange rate than their German counterparts. FX and Inflation | Rapid on energy, more progressive on core: Turning to inflation, there are potentially two channels leading to lower inflation after an appreciation of the euro. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 13 Returns differ: AI delivers durable productivity gains At the same time, AI investment offers a return profile distinct from property and traditional infrastructure. The marginal growth contribution from additional property investment is structurally low. To start with, roughly 30% of property investment consists of land purchases, which are excluded from capital formation in GDP accounting. Meanwhile, the return on each yuan of investment has declined sharply as the country builds up a large housing stock. AI capex, by contrast, involves minimal land cost: data centers are typically built on industrial land, which is substantially cheaper than residential land and often leased or subsidized by local governments. Beyond accounting, AI investment reinforces China’s position at the global technological frontier and delivers broad‑based productivity gains with a more durable long‑term return profile. A growing literature finds that AI‑related innovation has a disproportionately large impact on TFP— critical for sustaining potential growth as China’s labor force contracts. These productivity‑enhancing spillovers imply a more stable growth trajectory over time, even as the overall value of FAI steps down. Two waves of AI investment will reshape the FAI mix We expect AI‑related investment to unfold in two waves, with uneven effects on productivity across sectors. records.text: on current valuations, the model suggests January’s MBS overweights to decline by 2.5% from December to 7.2% (Figure 13). An MBS overweight of 7.2% would imply a 5.1% reduction in allocation over the coming months. However, we think the following considerations should be kept in mind while assessing the change in allocation from here: nViews on IG corporates: although MBS spreads have tightened, money managers may still be reluctant to increase allocation to corporates given spreads remain at historic tights. This suggests the model error will persist, and allocation may only go down by 2.5% versus the 5.1% reduction the model output of 7.2% implies. nHigher mortgage rates likely lead to more policy actions and difficult to hedge prepay risk: MBS investors are now acutely aware of policy risks like a g-fee/FHA MIP cut. Simply speaking, we think policy risk will increase if mortgage rates trend higher and decrease if mortgage rates trend lower. This point towards elevated and difficult to hedge refi risk. Given most of the overweights are in higher coupons (Figure 14), we think the policy risk could lead to a larger reduction in overweights than the 2.5% implied by the model. records.text: l January level. The second historical episode took place during the winter of 2022–23, following the sharp reduction in Russian gas supplies to Europe. In response to the heightened risk of physical gas shortages, the European Union introduced emergency energy-security measures, including the mandatory 15% gas-demand reduction target under the “Save Gas for a Safe Winter” regulation. Gas consumption was shaped by administrative prioritization rather than market pricing, with policymakers aiming to preserve physical gas availability for the winter period. This caused temporary fuel switching and the limited use of dual-fuel and oil-fired units, lifting oil-based power generation to a peak of around 1.3 GW in January 2023. This level of generation is equivalent to approximately 50 kbd of fuel oil demand, even under stressed market conditions. Since then, oil-fired power generation has remained structurally depressed, with utilization not exceeding 0.6 GW, or roughly 25 kbd, over the past two years (Figure 22). records.text: European Rates Weekly 30 January 2026 Citi Research 13 Primary demand: No signs of investor fatigue Primary demand for SSAs and covered bonds has increased strongly since 2020 with prior years’ record-high subscriptions only to be breached the following years. In 2026, this trend has not only continued but also accelerated. In SSAs, aggregate bid-to-cover ratios for € SSAs have more than quadrupled from pre-pandemic levels whilst for $ SSAs they have tripled (Figure 21). In January 2026, € deals have been on 8x over-subscribed, whilst $ deals also attracted nearly five times more demand than was issued. Similarly, in € covered bonds, the aggregate bid-to-cover ratio reached an all-time high of 4.0x in January as primary supply did not keep up with investor demand (Figure 22). Whilst the continued tightening of SSA and covered bond swap spreads and their outperformance of government bonds since 2022, particularly in €, has raised some questions on how long the investor demand will hold up, thus far we are not seeing any signs of investor fatigue. In fact, the reception of YTD primary supply argues the contrary. Figure 21. We think there would be very little support on the committee to move away from ample and back to scarce, but within this framework there is a bit of wiggle room. Balance sheet background: where are we now? The balance sheet has been a major focus for Fed policy makers over the past few months as it had been reducing its security holdings for several years as it aimed to reach an “ample" level – enough reserves in the system so that swings in its nonreserve liabilities still keep enough reserves in the system so that they do not move into scarcity. In December, the Fed determined that reserve levels had reached "ample, " as funding pressures emerged in the fourth quarter and started a program to increase its holdings of T-bills to maintain this ample level over time. Why does the Fed hold so many assets? It's all about the liabilities. The Fed has several major categories of liabilities beyond reserves on its balance sheet, which are backed by assets such as UST coupons and increasingly T-bills. records.text: businesses.” The Fed’s balance sheet Warsh’s views likely differ the most from those of current Fed officials on the topic of balance sheet policy. He opposed the Fed’s QE2 program and resigned from the Fed after it was announced. Since then, he has been a frequent critic of the Fed’s balance sheet, noting that it remains far larger than it was before the 2008 financial crisis, and he continued to call for shrinking it over the last year. Warsh has offered several arguments for reducing the balance sheet. First, that the Fed has too large of a role in financial markets and should aim to stay out of asset markets outside of crises. Second, that past asset purchase programs caused a “misallocation of capital” by “redirecting capital from the real domestic economy to financial assets” and have “been a material part of the inequality story.” Third, that the larger balance sheet contributes to higher inflation. And fourth, that the Fed’s asset holdings have “subsidized” the government’s financing costs, enabling fiscal policymakers to run larger deficits. Most Fed policymakers and members of the Fed staff would likely take a different view on these points. They see the growth of the balance sheet relative to the size of the economy as a necessary consequence of faster growth in demand for the Fed’s liabilities and the switch to an ample reserves framework for implementing monetary policy. The Nikkei and Yomiuri newspapers reported on Thursday that the LDP is gaining momentum at the beginning of the campaign, and Polymarket indicates that the probability of the LDP winning a majority (scenario A or B in our note) stands at 74% as of today, an increase from approximately 50% before Wednesday. If our scenario study is correct, the initial market reaction after the election is likely to reflect an extension of the Takaichi trade (equity prices up, JPY depreciates, and JGB yields up). However, we noted that the market reaction would reverse after the initial reaction as market participants come to recognise the government will find it more challenging to implement aggressive fiscal policies , especially a cut in consumption tax, immediately. The FY2026 budget draft was already presented at the end of last year and needs to pass the Diet as soon as possible for the new fiscal year, which starts in April. It means that amending the FY2026 budget, including the tax cut, is difficult. On the dovish side, inflation picked up in December but was below the BoE’s expectations, unemployment is higher, and wage growth is tracking slightly lower vs. BoE’s forecasts. Assuming a similar m/m increase for wages in December as in November, Q4 wage growth could be 3.4%, lower than the BoE projection of 3.5%. The BoE would incorporate the impact of the Autumn Budget measures in its forecasts. Budget measures are likely to lower Q2 2026 inflation by ~50bps and push up 2027/28 inflation by 10bps. We expect 2026Q1 inflation to be revised down from 3.1% to 3.0% and 2026Q2 inflation to be revised down from 2.9% to 2.3%. Overall, we expect the BoE to revise down 2026 inflation from 2.8% to 2.4%. Medium term inflation is likely to reduce slightly: we expect 20281Q and 20291Q inflation at 2.0% (down from 2.1%). BoE’s gradual guidance, pickup in inflation, better sentiment data and elevated price/wage expectations rule out a back-to-back cut. And while the labour market continues to soften, in our view, it’s not deteriorating rapidly enough for a back- to-back cut. In December, the BoE emphasized more caution as they approach close to neutral, with decisions on future cuts becoming a closer call. 7-2 vote with risks of a 6-3 We expect a 7-2 vote for a hold, with Taylor and Dhingra voting for a 25bps cut. There are risks of a 6-3 vote with Ramsden voting for a 25bps cut. Previously, Ramsden has voted twice for a back-to-back cut (Dec 2024, June 2025) which implies it is possible that he votes for a cut next week on the back of softer labour market. But in December, he noted that there could be scope to slow the easing cadence in due course, which in our view signals that he likely votes for a hold in February. Similarly, Breeden noted that greater accumulation of evidence on disinflation is needed, which likely implies a hold. records.text: Potential Increase to Foreign Ownership Limit a Positive, But Not Durable Catalyst Saudi Arabia a notable laggard in EM in 2025 Saudi Arabia has been a notable laggard in EM equities since 2025 (MSCI Saudi Arabia: 0% vs MSCI EM: +40%) driven by a weak oil price environment, tight domestic liquidity in the banking sector, and announcements of a re-prioritization of fiscal spending plans, which have together weighed on investor sentiment. While YTD performance has been relatively strong on the back of higher commodity prices, for 2026 as a whole, our commodity strategists expect oil prices to trend weaker (2026 averages of $56/bbl for Brent and $52 for WTI), which should continue to weigh on performance for the market. Similarly, our economists expect GDP growth to slow to 4.2% in 2026, below consensus expectations of 4.5%, and forecast a wider fiscal deficit than the official budget projections (6% vs 3.3% of GDP). Against this backdrop, the MSCI Saudi Arabia index continues to underperform our macro-model-implied performance despite the YTD rally. Increase in Foreign Ownership Limit (FOL) a near-term catalyst While the overall macro picture for Saudi Arabian equities looks challenging, an increase in the foreign ownership limit (FOL) on listed companies (from 49% currently) remains a potential catalyst — as it could result in higher weights in EM and global benchmarks, driving passive inflows. Similarly, inflation in rents, which also tend to see infrequent resets (though less concentrated in January) , should continue to ease this year and moderating ‘catch-up’ pressure is one factor behind the expected easing in y/y services inflation , b oth in January and on average this year. Government measures will be an important source of service price changes this month. Examples include a VAT hike in the Netherlands which is expected to push up y/y inflation for accommodation services ; a VAT cut on food services in restaurants in Germany and a cut in the reduced rate in Finland are downside risks, though pass-through for tax-cuts has often been low in the past ; there are increases in special railway tickets scheduled in several countries, but on average these are not expected to be higher than last year. records.text: Kevin Warsh on Interest Rate Policy, Balance Sheet Policy, and Financial Regulation President Trump announced on Friday that he will nominate Kevin Warsh to be the next Chair of the Federal Reserve. Warsh was previously a Fed governor from 2006-2011 and is currently a partner at Duquesne Family Office, a Visiting Fellow at the Hoover Institution, and a lecturer at the Stanford Graduate School of Business. Warsh will require Senate confirmation to become Chair. Senator Tillis, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, has reiterated that he will oppose the confirmation of any Fed nominee until the Department of Justice’s investigation into Chair Powell is resolved. Opposition from one Republican member of the committee is enough to stall the nomination if no Democrats on the committee support it. If the investigation is resolved, Warsh would likely be able to win the votes needed for confirmation. Financial markets reacted to the appointment with a small rise in long-term bond yields, a rebound in the US dollar, and a drop in precious metals prices. The move in bond yields likely reflected Warsh’s views on the Fed’s balance sheet, discussed below. We discuss Warsh’s recent views on the economic outlook, interest rate policy, the Fed’s balance sheet, and financial regulation below. records.text: M Idea 8 Staying the course on the balance sheet The Fed's implementation notice, released alongside the FOMC statement, affirmed no changes in its balance sheet policy: • Securities holdings in the SOMA portfolio will increase primarily through purchases of T-bills in order to maintain an ample level of reserves. • All principal payments of agency mortgage-backed securities will continue to be reinvested into T-bills. There was no discussion on balance sheet policies in Chair Powell’s press conference. In an environment where the Fed is increasing securities holdings and adding reserves to the financial system, we think it clearly lends to an opportunity set where investors should either be long or neutral expressions for richer (softer) funding. • Given the potential for RMP sizes to be flexed up, based on the outlook for the supply of reserve balances and market conditions, we do not deem the risk-reward of expressions for cheaper funding as attractive. We continue to suggest investors stay long 2y UST SOFR swap spreads, a view we have maintained since early October (see Exhibit 9 ). As shown in Exhibit 10 , the positive carry and rolldown characteristics of 2y spreads make this any easier position to hold, while waiting for a breakout to new highs. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 11 skewed to the downside, we think that March could move towards a ~50/50 cut probability, and April pricing could drift closer to ~20bp. Overall, we see the potential for markets to discount slightly above two 25bp cuts in 2026 following this scenario. The most prominent hawkish risk would be the BoE signalling that it is close to the end of the easing cycle, arguing that Bank Rate is approaching neutral. We view this as unlikely, as the BoE will likely want to preserve optionality, but such messaging could compress expectations towards only one cut this year and push timing out from April and into 2H26, for example towards July. Meanwhile, a 7-2 vote split could (at least temporarily) take March off the table, with April repricing to just below a 50/50 cut scenario and the market pricing out ~5bp of cumulative cuts in 2026. On the forecast set, we expect inflation to be broadly at target in 2026 and likely to remain there over the forecast horizon. We also expect BoE staff to level-shift the unemployment forecast higher by around 20bp (marking to market), embedding a peak jobless rate of ~5.3% in 2Q26. Consistent with this, we expect the output gap profile to show an average widening of roughly ~20bp of excess supply through the forecast horizon. records.text: nnouncements. The BoJ has got more work to do; pay 6m fwd 5y JPY and 5s30s ratio flattener (3x1). All roads eventually lead to the BoJ. Without further tightening, it’s likely FX and super long end sector rates weakness will persist. The last BoJ meeting was deemed ‘slightly hawkish’ by our rates strategist, as the risk balance for the economy was revised upward, and there was a hawkish dissent for a 25bp hike by board member Takata. The dissent is reminiscent of the September BoJ meeting, when board members Takata and Tamura voted for a 25bp hike, then executed after the LDP election in December. Expectations have now risen for a hike in April, priced close to ~20bps. We think the market will continue to expect a higher terminal rate for the BoJ, closer to 2%. We like to be paid in Japan rates, the pace may remain cautious, so we add a paid position in 5y space. The 5y point has richened on the 2s5s10s fly, we prefer to sell here. We also think a lot of the election and fiscal premiums have been priced now. We have warmed up to the idea of flatteners but are wary of risks of sharp sell-offs in the super long sector where demand may remain weak until elections. Hence, we also like to add a 3:1 DV01 ratio 6m fwd 5s30s flattener: $30k DV01 in 5y, and $10k in 30y. We think a DV01 weighted flattener will allow more staying power, to protect against term premia shocks. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 11 In the near term we expect inflation to be revised lower due to the recent undershoot, stronger sterling and Budget measures, offset slightly by lower Bank Rate path. The BoE would incorporate the impact of the Autumn Budget measures in its forecasts. Budget measures are likely to lower Q2 2026 inflation by ~50bps and push up 2027/28 inflation by 10bps. We expect 2026Q1 inflation to be revised down from 3.1% to 3.0% and 2026Q2 inflation to be revised down from 2.9% to 2.3%. Overall, we expect the BoE to revise down 2026 inflation from 2.8% to 2.4%. Medium term inflation is likely to reduce slightly: we expect 20281Q and 20291Q inflation at 2.0% (down from 2.1%). Near term growth could be pushed up slightly by 10-20bps to reflect the near-term fiscal loosening, with backloaded tax rises weighing on growth beyond the BoE’s three-year horizon. While recent ECB research shows that alternative approaches going beyond traditional filtering methods point to a somewhat smaller gap, it also highlights that a combination of cyclical and structural factors is weighing on the recovery in credit creation. Beyond the effects of elevated uncertainty and persistently higher interest rates relative to the pre-pandemic period, shifts in consumption patterns towards services and a growing share of investment directed towards intangible assets may partially explained the gap. As underlined in the December meeting accounts, subdued credit growth to firms and households may also reflect a shift in banks' asset-allocation strategies, with a greater focus on bond purchases and lending to non-bank financial intermediaries. Next week's releases – the survey on the access to finance of enterprises (SAFE, due 2 February) and the Q4 25/Q1 26 Bank Lending Survey (BLS, due 3 February) – will be key inputs for the Governing Council's assessment of transmission effectiveness. THEME OF THE WEEK: ASIA LOOKS DIFFERENT Although aggregate cross -asset volatility in EM remains low compared with prior cycles, this headline measure conceals a sharp divergence when we compare FX implied volatility across the three regions . EM Asia — traditionally regarded as the most resilient sub -region due to its current account surpluses and sizeable reserve buffers—has seen that status erode over the past year. Persistent trade-war tensions, sizable portfolio outflows, and central bank interventions have added layers of uncertainty, contributing to Asia’s underperformance vs EM despite a softer USD backdrop. With valuations still attractive and positioning relatively light, the key question for 2026 is whether Asia begins to reverse these headwinds, or whether the region remains an underperformer as geopolitical and policy risks continue to dominate the narrative. However, China LNG imports remain below those of January 2024, when temperatures were well in line with average. While we think high current LNG prices relative to 2024 play a role dampening imports, the surge in renewable generation has also likely weighed on gas demand. More agile framework for authorizing external debt would reduce crowding out Among these reforms, the bill to expedite the approval of external debt is crucial. Currently, any financing from external creditors (Eurobonds, multilaterals, bilaterals, foreign banks) requires two, two-thirds majority votes in Congress. This sometimes leads to a suboptimal financing strategy in which the government overlies on the domestic market to cover its needs, bidding up interest rates and crowing out private borrowers. The reform proposal is to expedite the external debt approval by embedding it in the budget, so it happens automatically when legislators vote on the budget. Other reforms: privatization, labor, tax, infrastructure Other key reforms that could materialize, in our view, are: i) the privatization of the second-largest commercial bank (Banco de Costa Rica, BCR), ii) labor reform (“ley 4-3”) to have more flexibility in work arrangements, iii) the “global income tax” which was discussed during the time of the IMF program, and iv) changes to the Public Procurement Law with an eye on speeding up infrastructure projects such as “Government City” (centralizing the main government buildings in a specific area of the capital), the Limon Pier, among others. While not our baseline, we see four potential avenues to negative rates: 1. Contrary to our expectations, the SNB could refrain from FX interventions and mainly use the policy rate to counter CHF strength. Our updated monthly tracker shows no meaningful net FX purchases between May and December (latest data). While we would not exclude discretionary purchases in January, we could be overestimating the SNB's willingness to intervene. 2. The state of the Swiss economy and (domestic) inflation pressures could turn out to be weaker than expected, requiring an even more expansionary policy stance. 3. Neutral could be lower than we (and the SNB) think so that the SNB could come to the conclusion that the current policy stance is not expansionary. In our view, this comes down to the question of whether the rate differential is sufficiently high in a world where increased geopolitical uncertainty may or may not alter CHF demand. 4. An external shock could hit, changing the fundamental outlook. One example would be a shock that changes ECB expectations towards cuts to well below 2% as this would compress the Swiss rate differential and likely trigger more persistent CHF appreciation. The neutral rate debate is shifting into higher gear With the economic outlook improving, we think the most important question for the Fed this year will be: where is the neutral rate, and how is it impacted by growing evidence of accelerating labor productivity? records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW Given the diversity of the countries under analysis, we explored whether maintaining equal weights for all components, as we do for our US and eurozone FCIs, was still suitable . After controlling for the expected relationship between each component and financial conditions – for example, higher equity prices are expected to lead to looser financial conditions –, we allowed our quantitative analysis to determine the optimal weights for each component. We do this by maximizing the correlation between our estimated FCI and lagged GDP growth across time (based on 2000–26 data). To avoid over-optimisation and data mining, we add an extra qualitative overlay to our analysis, leveraging the expertise of M360 strategists and economists. The final weights selection, which is shown in Figure 2, highlights how local equities, FX and commodities (when included) are considered the most relevant components for most countries under analysis. records.text: M Idea 4 Scenarios, topical policy issues and policy rules: With the output gap widening as medium-term inflation forecasts stay broadly unchanged, we think that the forward- looking policy rules presented in the model-based policy simulations in the November MPR can come down a touch (by ~10bp). Contemporaneous-style policy rules as well as the optimal policy projection will likely shift lower more notably, aligning more closely with the forward-looking policy approaches. We assume that the BoE will present the same two scenarios as was the case in the November MPR – one embedding inflation persistence, and another weaker demand. There could, we assume, be some changes in the "topical policy issues" which anchored the debate in the meeting minutes in November. For one, since as early as 1Q26, CPI inflation will likely be forecast to fall below the median estimate of the threshold for changes in the CPI inflation regime (i.e., below 3.1%Y), we see little point in the Box C ("Prospects for CPI inflation when inflation is high"). The MPC's focus on the so-called threshold effects (and, relatedly, spot inflation) should thus be softened as inflation slips below 3%Y. We suspect that the staff could instead revisit their estimates of how trade diversion might impact UK (core goods) inflation. The inflation release will be followed by the ECB meeting on Thursday. We expect the ECB to remain on hold next week. We do not think the Council is at a point yet where it would be ready to embrace the case for further rate cuts or signal hikes. For now, all options are still on the table. On the macro outlook, growth came in broadly in line with our expectations for 4Q25, but surveys do not point to an acceleration at the start of 2026. On inflation, different factors (realised data, higher oil & natural gas prices, stronger euro) have been pushing in different directions since December. The January print released the day before the meeting will clearly be key and we think it will point to downside risks to the December forecasts - see more here. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS The curious case of the US dollar The weakness of the US dollar is in vogue these days, but we think part of the narrative is overblown. US exceptionalism has allowed sustained current account and fiscal deficits to be easily financed at low interest rates while leading to a historically strong dollar as capital flowed to the US. Despite uncertainty and policy changes, the relative outperformance of the US shows no signs of cracking. True, the dollar may have lost some of its luster, including its hedging properties, and some further depreciation may follow. But there are limits to how much depreciation could take place, not least because monetary policy abroad would react to it. And if the story is about fiscal profligacy and dollar (and other currencies’) debasement, then we should be asking ourselves how much more room to run real assets may have. US exceptionalism as the driver of US dollar strength The US dollar had been remarkably strong for several years until 2025. Policy uncertainty and changes in the US have arguably led to the dollar slide since last year, not least because of the pre-existing crowded positioning in US assets (Exhibit 1). Another issue for next week is the potential for a partial government shutdown being triggered this weekend as appropriations are set to lapse for some key parts of the federal government. That said, it is important to remember that government shutdowns are distinct from debt limit impasses. In a shutdown, government spending is affected via the authority to spend money, but not the Treasury's ability to issue debt or pay interest. Last year we had both a government shutdown and a debt limit impasse, and investors often conflate the two. The debt limit was resolved as part of the OBBBA, which raised the limit by $5tn. That gave Treasury enough borrowing capacity to carry it at least through the end of 2027. The government shutdown last year was resolved with the passage of full-year appropriations for some agencies, but others only saw continued funding until January 30. Agencies whose funding lapses at the end of this month include the IRS. What does a partial government shutdown mean for the front-end? The effect is largely seen through potentially lower net outflows from the TGA, meaning that the TGA is a touch higher than otherwise would have been the case if the government was fully funded. records.text: US Treasury’s FX Report removes calls for rate hikes while identifying fiscal expansion as a driver of JPY weakness Meanwhile, the US Treasury released its semiannual Report on Macroeconomic and Foreign Exchange Polices on the 29th. The previous report had stated that “BoJ policy tightening should continue to proceed in response to domestic economic fundamentals […], supporting a normalization of the yen’s weakness against the dollar and a much-needed structural rebalancing of bilateral trade. ” but this language was completely removed in the latest edition. While Treasury Secretary Bessent had previously urged continued rate hikes to correct JPY weakness and had pressed the Takaichi administration not to interfere with the BoJ, the tide appears to be turning. Furthermore, the latest report identified not only interest‑rate differentials but also “the prospects for more expansionary fiscal policies under a new Japanese government” as one of the main drivers of JPY depreciation. In the market, there was growing speculation that Japan incurred a “debt of gratitude” to the US for the coordinated rate check and that the US might demand early BoJ rate hikes in return. However, judging from the latest Report, such concerns now appear limited. For the BoJ, although it cannot relax its vigilance around JPY weakness, which continues to fuel inflation, the easing of external pressure may provide greater policy flexibility. records.text: What about the funding and design of the proposed consumption tax cut? The first issue surrounding the consumption tax cut is the annual JPY4.8trn in funding. Although both the LDP and the CRA continue to say they will not rely on deficit‑financing bonds, they offer little in the way of concrete details. Takaichi has cited the use of non‑tax revenues and the streamlining of special tax measures and subsidies as potential funding sources, but specifics remain entirely unclear. Meanwhile, the CRA has outlined a plan to establish a JPY500trn “government fund” (SWF), using its investment returns as the funding source. According to the original proposal by Komeito, this fund would be backed by public financial assets such as those of the GPIF, the BoJ’s ETF holdings, and the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account. However, the challenges are immense, ranging from the risks of using FX‑intervention funds, governance concerns, and, most critically, whether it is appropriate to rely on inherently volatile market returns as a permanent source of revenue for a tax cut. Furthermore, although the LDP positions the measure as temporary for two years, it may be politically difficult to retract it once households have benefited. With an upper house election scheduled for the summer of 2028, postponement may be the more likely outcome. The second issue concerns system design. Under the assumption of a nominal neutral rate around 1% or slightly below (in line with the SNB’s r* estimate of around zero), the SNB’s policy stance has likely started to turn expansionary with the cut to 0.5% in December 2024 and been clearly expansionary since the policy rate reached 0% in June 2025. This means we are still in the transmission phase, and the impact should become visible over the course of the year. Hence from a growth and inflation point of view, there would seem no reason for the SNB to cut rates further. FX intervention as first line of defence Our policy rate forecast is complemented by our longstanding view that the first line of defence against CHF strength would be discretionary FX interventions. While the SNB usually notes that the policy rate is the primary instrument, it also stresses its preparedness to purchase FX "if needed". The large FX intervention of CHF 5bn last April (when the US tariff shock led to upward pressure on the CHF) is a key example. In our view, FX interventions in the current setting are primarily discretionary, i.e. aimed at countering safe haven flows rather than permanently easing the monetary policy stance. According to SNB estimates, every 27bn of purchases depreciates the CHF by 1.1%. In turn, this implies that prices can also hold higher than we thought previously. The increase in physical demand late last year, notably from India during the festive season as well as the Middle East, is now also being seen in China. We are hearing of an increase in physical investment interest, as retail consumers turn to the more affordable alternative to gold. With silver inventories in SHFE warehouses having been drawn down in the past several years, restocking alongside this increase in demand is likely manifesting in the unusual silver onshore premiums in China. The first wave will be capex‑heavy, driven by large‑scale build‑outs of IT infrastructure, electricity generation and transmission, and high‑tech manufacturing. The second wave will come from large‑scale deployment of AI across services—finance, education, healthcare, and public administration. Much of this spending in the initial stage will take the form of opex rather than capex, but it is likely to deliver broader and larger growth dividends. Knowledge‑intensive sectors to see higher TFP gains and more labor disruption Productivity gains will vary widely by sector. Most estimates point to the largest TFP increases in knowledge‑intensive services. Technology services, finance, and professional services could see 2–3pp annual TFP gains, well above the 0.1–0.2pp expected in manual‑intensive sectors such as transport, retail, and parts of construction, according to OECD estimates 1. As a result, AI‑driven investment in knowledge‑intensive services is likely to deliver the strongest productivity boost. However, large TFP gains do not automatically translate into rapid aggregate growth. Baumol’s cost disease remains a constraint: a large share of employment is concentrated in labor‑intensive services where output is harder to scale. records.text: ponement may be the more likely outcome. The second issue concerns system design. Broadly, it would follow one of two patterns: (1) a zero tax rate (exemption) or (2) non-taxation. Under the former, businesses can receive refunds through input‑tax credits, but the government must shoulder all fiscal costs and heavy administrative burdens. Also, businesses would need to bridge cash flow until refunds are paid. Under the latter, businesses cannot receive refunds. As a result, while the government burden is reduced, the measure effectively becomes a tax increase for businesses, possibly making it harder to lower retail prices, thus limiting households’ ability to fully enjoy the benefits of the tax cut. At present, both the LDP and the CRA appear to be aiming for the “zero tax rate” structure. However, as noted above, the government would need to cover all fiscal costs and a vast amounts of refund administration, while numerous businesses would likely face cash‑flow impediments, making it unlikely that these hurdles could be addressed quickly. records.text: Economic outlook Warsh has made a few comments on the evolving balance of risks facing the US economy over the last two years. In the fall of 2024, he opposed interest rate cuts because he worried that the FOMC risked declaring victory over inflation prematurely. In 2025, he argued that the Trump administration’s deregulatory policies and potential spending cuts would be disinflationary enough to outweigh any one-time effect of tariffs on prices, which the Fed could look through anyway. More recently, he said that the US economy “could be at the front end of a productivity boom” driven by artificial intelligence (AI). As a result, he said, “We are probably in the early innings of a structural decline in prices. AI is going to make almost everything cost less.” Because he thinks that “ AI will be a significant disinflationary force,” he has argued that the Fed should not keep interest rates high solely in response to strong GDP growth. Instead, he said, the FOMC should imitate the approach taken under the leadership of former Chairman Alan Greenspan in the 1990s, when strong GDP growth was powered by strong productivity growth that was “structurally disinflationary.” Interest rate policy Warsh’s less concerned take on the inflation picture might position him on the dovish side of the FOMC’s current policy debate. records.text: ices The Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand increased by 0.5% in December, up from 0.1% in October and 0.2% in November, exceeding both our forecast and the consensus estimate of a 0.2% rise for December. The strength was in the services portion — particularly the trade services portion, which tends to be volatile and rebounded by 1.7% in December after declining by 0.8% in October and 0.6% in November. In contrast, prices for final demand goods remained unchanged due to declines in food and energy prices, which fell by 0.3% and 1.4%, respectively, over the month. That said, the strength was not all in trade services. The core PPI—which excludes food, energy, and volatile trade services—increased by 0.4% in December, higher than the 0.2% gain reported in November but lower than 0.7% gain in October. Core goods— which exclude the volatile categories of food and energy—rose by 0.4%, slightly above the six-month average of 0.3%. Capital equipment prices advanced 0.4%, consistent with the 0.2%–0.5% range observed throughout 2025. This report has been prepared by UBS Securities LLC. records.text: Looking ahead to 2026, Eurosystem staff projections envisage growth of 0.3% q/q in Q1, followed by a pick-up to 0.4% q/q over the remainder of the year. So far, however, incoming high-frequency indicators for January do not point to a firming in momentum at the start of the year. PMIs entered Q1 around 0.8 pt below their Q4 25 average, alongside signs of a rotation in the composition of growth, with manufacturing improving on the one hand, and services momentum softening on the other. Ultimately, meeting the ECB's December projections will depend on a continued strengthening in domestic demand, led by both private consumption and investment. The outlook for consumers remains subdued, with households' consumption decelerating since mid-2024 despite rising real income. Elevated geopolitical uncertainty could continue to weigh on consumers' confidence and lead to a slower normalisation of the savings ratio than forecast by the ECB staff. This could be reinforced by Ricardian behaviour in countries where fiscal deficits are either on an upward trajectory (Germany) or remain stubbornly elevated (France). Several factors support the ECB's forecast for a marked strengthening in investment: the lagged pass-through of monetary policy easing, increased digital investment as firms accelerate technology adoption – including AI – and substantial public spending on infrastructure and defence. Takafumi YamawakiAC (81-3) 6736-1748 takafumi.yamawaki@jpmorgan.com Hiroki Yagi(81-3) 6736-6783 hiroki.yagi@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy Japan Fixed Income Markets Weekly 30 January 2026 J P M O R G A N At the beginning of this month, we highlighted an interesting development in the BoJ’s collateral data, which registered a near JPY2tn increase in December (on a face value basis), despite a JPY4tn decline in the outstanding balance of the Funds-Provisioning Measure to Stimulate Bank Lending. While the underlying cause remains unclear, we suggested that it may be related to Thursday’s operation, which attracted solid demand, as widely anticipated. Additionally, we noted that the monthly average of the daily peak of intraday overdrafts could be a source of an increase in posted collateral at the central bank. However, the monthly settlement statistics released this week show that intraday overdrafts remained within recent ranges, and as a result, the collateral utilization rate moved lower in December (Figure 6C o l l a t e r a l u t i l i z a t i o n s u n k t o t h e l o w e s t l e v e l i n D e c e m b e r ). Banks continue to post solid beats driven by capital markets activity, yet the lack of meaningful lending growth has kept analysts from raising forward expectations. Meanwhile, consumer companies continue to cite weak demand, challenges tied to U.S. tariffs and pronounced currency volatility. Two sectors, however, have captured analysts’ attention and received meaningful upgrades to their 2026 earnings forecasts: Materials—driven primarily by Miners benefiting from rising metal prices —and, unsurprisingly, Technology. Tech company reports continue to highlight insatiable AI‑related demand, and the extraordinary Capex commitments across the industry all but guarantee strong and, importantly, highly predictable earnings for Hardware and Semiconductor names. Institutional investors have accordingly built sizable positions in these areas and show little inclination to unwind them (Figure 4). Software, by contrast, tells a very different story: institutional investors have been reducing exposure, hedge funds are building short positions, and concerns about monetization are rising. This persistent scepticism underscores investors’ extremely low tolerance for any hint of earnings softness, making it increasingly unlikely that the equity rally will broaden meaningfully beyond the narrow group of super‑earnings leaders anytime soon. In that context, the Governing Council (GC) emphasised that it was important to retain maximum optionality, reaffirming a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach and avoiding forward guidance. Ahead of the February meeting, while incoming data have broadly been consistent with December staff projections, the risks factors that Lagarde listed have deteriorated, in our assessment. Three developments stand out. First, on the geopolitical front the tariff flare-up tied to Greenland's sovereignty, even if now temporarily de-escalated, was a blunt reminder of how fragile the US–Europe agenda remains and how quickly trade risks can re-emerge. Second, China's import volumes and import price dynamics have likely intensified concerns about the "second China shock" as was discussed at the December gathering. Lastly, renewed dollar softness has lifted EUR/USD by roughly 3% against the December technical assumptions, which will drag on inflation, economic activity and magnify concerns about euro area competitive disadvantages. records.text: Global FX 29 January 2026 Citi Research 2 Q1: Will there be concerted intervention by the Japanese and US governments? We do not at this point expect concerted intervention by Japan and the US. Last week the NY Fed apparently conducted rate checks, as reported by the WSJ on January 23. This made it clear that US authorities support the Takaichi government’s policy to defend the JPY and hints that US intervention may be closer than generally thought. However, since the 2000s the general policy of G7 countries has been not to intervene in forex markets when unnecessary. We do not think the US will intervene to support Japan by selling the USD while it has no particular economic reason of its own. Q2: Has concerted intervention been effective in the past? Figure 1 shows the Bollinger Bands of the five-year average for the JPY real effective exchange rate (REER). As was the case after the earthquake and tsunami of 2011, there has been concerted intervention by G7 nations when this JPY index has move by 2σ or more toward either JPY strength (USD weakness) or JPY weakness (USD strength). Such interventions have tended to cause a turnaround in the long-term trend in the JPY. Whatever the theoretical background, in practice concerted intervention seems to be effective in engineering a turnaround in forex rate trends. Figure 1. What is perhaps most interesting is the decoupling between the dollar and US interest rates. In our view, this reflects that the dollar may have lost some of its hedging appeal, as it has not performed as a safe haven in the event of US-specific policy risks. In other words, the decoupling between the dollar and US interest rates could be a sign of US- specific risk premium. The limits to real dollar depreciation Despite the decoupling between the dollar and interest rates, and the dollar’s slide in the past year, there are limits to how much real dollar depreciation can be. Even after the recent dollar depreciation and the further move we may expect, the dollar remains about equally strong in real terms as three years ago (Exhibit 3). So what are the limits we have in mind? A large real depreciation of the dollar vis-à-vis other currencies would be a recessionary shock for the global economy ex-US. And while some economies with strong momentum could withstand it well, most developed economies would not emerge unscathed. With a general equilibrium view, weaker global ex-US growth and the subsequent monetary policy easing amid deflationary pressures would give a floor. After seasonal adjustment (which expects a larger swing from hiring to firing), the result is a boost to January payrolls. In our forecast, retail payrolls rebound from -25k in December to +30k in January. Transport and warehousing payrolls swing from falling to flat. In the other direction, we expect a 40k decline in federal government payrolls. The deferred resignation program (DRP), originally aimed at October resignations, appears to have been extended somewhat and perhaps enlarged somewhat. OPM Director Kupor indicated that about ⅔ of the resignations occurred in September, with the remaining ⅓ at the end of the year. We have also seen commentary that the total size of the program was somewhat larger than the 150k estimate. We've allowed 40k in layoffs in January simply because the October decline in federal government payrolls, -160k, was so large. There's risk in both directions for the federal government payrolls forecast: that for some reason the October payrolls report picked up the full DRP. Or that the program was larger than we recognized and resulted in more resignations at the end of December. In the one case, Federal employment decline could be near zero; in the other, as large as 70k. We estimate average hourly earnings rose 0.2% m/m, held back partially by the shift back toward lower-wage industry payrolls, with the y/y pace slowing 0.2 pct

records.text: European Rates Weekly 30 January 2026 Citi Research 6 Against a backdrop of seemingly suppressed rates vol, carry-driven positioning in € 5s30s curve would have been quite profitable over the last year. Curiously enough, sticking to steepeners would have been profitable even in times of higher implied vol – suggesting that fiscal risk is becoming a major driver of risk appetite. We argue that, conditional on the sign of carry, this feature also extends to $ 5s30s – a stylized fact consistent with the fact that the correlation between € and $ current forward curves tends to systematically underestimate the one between future spot curves. In our latest European Rates Weekly, we noted that, over the last three years, episodes where realized vol spiked have not been met by losses on carry strategies deployed on € 5s30s. We tentatively interpreted such feature, which is limited to 5s30s and doesn’t apply to other slopes / flies on the € swap curve as a symptom of spikes in vol coinciding more and more a re-pricing of fiscal premia. In what follows, we try and gain a better understanding of this stylized fact. We believe that she would likely push for the same economic reforms that the Chaves administration couldn’t get done because of lack of support in Congress. More agile framework for authorizing external debt would reduce crowding out Among these reforms, the bill to expedite the approval of external debt is crucial. Currently, any financing from external creditors (Eurobonds, multilaterals, bilaterals, foreign banks) requires two, two-thirds majority votes in Congress. This sometimes leads to a suboptimal financing strategy in which the government overlies on the domestic market to cover its needs, bidding up interest rates and crowing out private borrowers. The reform proposal is to expedite the external debt approval by embedding it in the budget, so it happens automatically when legislators vote on the budget. Other reforms: privatization, labor, tax, infrastructure Other key reforms that could materialize, in our view, are: i) the privatization of the second-largest commercial bank (Banco de Costa Rica, BCR), ii) labor reform (“ley 4-3”) to have more flexibility in work arrangements, iii) the “global income tax” which was discussed during the time of the IMF program, and iv) changes to the Public Procurement Law with an eye on speeding up infrastructure projects such as “Government City” (centralizing the main government buildings in a specific area of the capital), the Limon Pier, among others. The "twisted Diet" and the situation in the House of Councillors (Upper House) Regardless of the election outcome, the new administration will likely face a difficult start due to a "twisted Diet" – a divided legislature where the ruling coalition lacks a majority in the House of Councillors (the Upper House) (Figure 4). This power dynamic creates significant legislative hurdles. Bills passed by the Lower House can be rejected by the Upper House. While the Lower House can override an Upper House veto with a two-thirds majority, securing such a supermajority is extremely difficult. As a result, the new government would be forced to negotiate with opposition parties to pass any legislation, a situation that would likely constrain policymaking until at least the 2028 Upper House election. Risk 1: External shock In our view, an unexpected shock is the most obvious source of changes to the SNB rate outlook, and the likelihood of external shocks is elevated in the current uncertain global environment. One consequential shock that we have frequently outlined before would be a one that rapidly alters the Eurozone inflation outlook and leads the ECB to cut rates well below 2% (or the market pricing such a scenario). This would compress the SNB- ECB rate differential and likely trigger more persistent CHF appreciation and deflationary pressure like in 2010-2022 (Figure 6S w i s s i n f l a t i o n a n d S N B - E C B r a t e d i f f e r e n t i a l ). records.text: M Idea 14 European Economics: FX and the Euro Area Jens Eisenschmidt and Jean-Francois Ouvrard • Most often, exchange rate shocks do not happen in isolation but reflect other "structural shocks", for instance changes to monetary or fiscal policies, which need to be considered in a broader assessment. • Looking only at the exchange rate channel, for growth, the main impact is through exports. A 5% appreciation of the euro in effective terms reduces EA exports by 1.5% and growth by 0.3pp on our estimates. • The transmission to consumer prices comes rapidly through energy prices (since oil is traded in USD) and, more progressively, core inflation. On our estimates, a 10% appreciation of the euro versus the dollar lowers inflation by 30bp in the next two years. The macro view on FX | That’s complex: In this section, we review implications of FX movements for the macro outlook in Europe. Before diving into some estimates, we want to highlight one key point: most of the time, exchange rate shocks do not happen in isolation. Rather they will likely reflect other "structural shocks" such as changes to monetary or fiscal policies domestically or abroad. For instance, FX might often be the most rapid channel of monetary policy when one compares it to the slow transmission from rates to aggregate domestic demand. So, while we can try and estimate the impacts of the economy from "pure" FX shocks "everything else unchanged", as we do below, the reality is likely much more complex. FX and

Amid concerns on Fed independence, increased geopolitical tensions and broader policy and political uncertainty, gold is acting as a relative safe-haven asset to help protect portfolios against various possible macro outcomes. The lack of strong conviction on any potential scenario makes it challenging to also have strong conviction across the various asset classes. Gold therefore stands out as one of the cleanest ways to position against US dollar weakness, broader concerns on fiat currencies, long-term worries about countries’ debt and fiscal deficits, lower real rates (either driven by sticky inflation and/or more dovish Fed), and potential policy missteps, to just name a few. Any shifts out of other asset classes, be it currencies, bonds or equities, could have a notable impact on gold, given the relative size of the market. This is because as Figure 5 shows, swap spread positions (long Treasury vs pay fixed in swaps) are positive carry across the curve. Because of this, substituting a given duration exposure in Treasuries with the same amount of exposure in a corresponding interest rate swap reduces the carry. Vol replication: Some examples When it comes to vol replication, the main issue tends to be which point on the vol surface to sell. Typically, because the vol-related risks are second order, an exact matching of all the exposures along the vol surface (using partial vegas or matched option profiles) is rare. Instead, the typical considerations boil down to how and whether to replicate all vol related risks (vega, gamma) or to just replicate the negative convexity. The reason for this is simple—swaptions with greater vega (longer expiry) tend to have smaller gamma. So one needs to choose the right expiry. Theoretically, it is possible to exactly match both the vega and the gamma of a given mortgage-backed security with a single expiry (for MBS close to current coupon, this would be somewhere between 1y10y and 3y10y). But moves in the underlying would cause the exact match to shift and a continuous matching of vega and gamma is difficult. records.text: 8 Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 We should probably expect, once again, the emphasis to be on the prevailing level of uncertainty. While this could be perceived as dovish, it would only reiterate the message given in December. Uncertainty is also likely to be the key reason for not providing any kind of forward guidance. Where do we go from here? Back in December, we argued that a March cut was still likely if data moved the way we expected. Our view was based on a combination of data surprises and the ECB’s concern about being perceived as asymmetric. Why are we less convinced about that cut today? The German contribution to Euro-area disinflation in 1Q26 is a little more uncertain than we had anticipated given some noise and volatile factors in the data. The downward surprise to ECB forecasts could be less pronounced. But we remain convinced of an easing bias. Only last week did the accounts of the December meeting reveal the first reference to the decoupling between market inflation fixings and ECB pricing in this context, which could mean some are noticing credibility issues in delivering on the inflation target. But March may be too early to expect action on this.

Economic outlook | Discussing risks: On the macro outlook, Governors will have a lot to catch up on since they last discussed projections in December. On growth, data are broadly in line with short-term expectations for 4Q25, but surveys do not point to an acceleration at the start of 2026 and some headwinds have likely strengthened, notably from trade uncertainties. On inflation, different factors (realised data, higher oil & natural gas prices, stronger euro) have been pushing in different directions since December. The January print released the day before the meeting will clearly be key. We think it will point to downside risks to the December forecasts. Rates Strategy | Assessing the inflation outlook.
