United States: Interest Rates Sleepy, no more We expect the yield curve to steepen as while concerns about Japanese investors selling USTs are overstated, a weaker dollar argues for more term premium. We recommend 5y5y breakeven longs. The Treasury is also likely to maintain the status quo and not cut long-end sizes as some have speculated. The US Treasury yield curve bull steepened despite a modestly hawkish FOMC outcome, amid a sharp sell-off in the USD and a modest correction in risk assets as Microsoft fell more than 10% on Thursday. Since Friday, 2y UST yields have fallen 5bp while 30y yields have risen 4bp, resulting in a material steepening of the yield curve ( Figure 1). In contrast, German government yields fell across the curve as markets digested the implications of a strong EUR on the ECB policy. The broad trade-weighted dollar fell sharply, now down 10% from the recent peak and back to the levels observed in 2022 ( Figure 2). We have been arguing for lower front-end yields and a steeper yield curve and we maintain those views. We believe that despite an upgrade of the economic outlook, the Fed retains an easing bias, which suggests that 1yf2y yields at 3.7% are high, both compared with the expected policy rate in a year's time and a benign inflation outlook. The weaker dollar, however, should limit the pass-through of lower fed funds rate to longer-term yields as inflation breakevens widen even as concerns about foreign investors stepping back remain at bay. records.text: 8 Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 We should probably expect, once again, the emphasis to be on the prevailing level of uncertainty. While this could be perceived as dovish, it would only reiterate the message given in December. Uncertainty is also likely to be the key reason for not providing any kind of forward guidance. Where do we go from here? Back in December, we argued that a March cut was still likely if data moved the way we expected. Our view was based on a combination of data surprises and the ECB’s concern about being perceived as asymmetric. Why are we less convinced about that cut today? The German contribution to Euro-area disinflation in 1Q26 is a little more uncertain than we had anticipated given some noise and volatile factors in the data. The downward surprise to ECB forecasts could be less pronounced. But we remain convinced of an easing bias. Only last week did the accounts of the December meeting reveal the first reference to the decoupling between market inflation fixings and ECB pricing in this context, which could mean some are noticing credibility issues in delivering on the inflation target. But March may be too early to expect action on this.

records.text: 10 Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 Minimal changes to gradual guidance, but dovish risks vs. market pricing We expect the gradual and meeting by meeting guidance to remain amid elevated price/wage expectations, with the extent of future cuts dependent on how the inflation outlook evolves. We also expect the BoE to emphasize that judgments around further cuts are becoming a closer call, as restrictiveness of policy has fallen, and rates approach close to neutral. We expect the guidance to remain unchanged from December “The extent of further easing in monetary policy will depend on the evolution of the outlook for inflation. The restrictiveness of policy has fallen as Bank Rate has been reduced by 150 basis points since August 2024. On the basis of the current evidence, Bank Rate is likely to continue on a gradual downward path. But judgements around further policy easing will become a closer call.” At the same time, we expect the easing bias to remain with the path of rates likely downwards. Relative to market pricing, we think risks are tilted towards a dovish surprise, which keeps the door open for a near term cut. Markets are pricing in a small chance of a March cut (which is currently our base case), 18bps by April and 23bps by June. At the same time terminal pricing has also moved up. As with our US and eurozone FCIs, we aim to provide a quantitative signal of how tight or loose financing conditions investors and the real economy face in each country. To construct the indices, we maintain our two-layer approach, looking at sub-components and aggregating them into a single index. There are two main differences with the methodology we apply to our US and eurozone FCIs though. ▪ We introduce commodities as a new component, as our analysis highlights its importance for evaluating financial conditions in commodity exporters such as Norway, Canada and Australia (see page 3). ▪ We assign different weights to different components, in contrast to the equally-weighted aggregation we use for US and eurozone FCIs (page 4). records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 5 We should probably expect, once again, the emphasis to be on the prevailing level of uncertainty. While this could be perceived as dovish, it would only reiterate the message given in December. Uncertainty is also likely to be the key reason for not providing any kind of forward guidance. Where do we go from here? Back in December, we argued that a March cut was still likely if data moved the way we expected. Our view was based on a combination of data surprises and the ECB’s concern about being perceived as asymmetric. Why are we less convinced about that cut today? The German contribution to Euro-area disinflation in 1Q26 is a little more uncertain than we had anticipated given some noise and volatile factors in the data. The downward surprise to ECB forecasts could be less pronounced. But we remain convinced of an easing bias. Only last week did the accounts of the December meeting reveal the first reference to the decoupling between market inflation fixings and ECB pricing in this context, which could mean some are noticing credibility issues in delivering on the inflation target. But March may be too early to expect action on this.

For this reason, we remain skeptical that policy will change in a discrete way in June once the leadership handoff takes place, especially since the chair has just one vote on a particularly divided committee. Warsh’s path to the Chair seat From the Trump administration’s perspective, the clearest path to a more dovish Committee that can deliver lower rates would be to place Warsh in Chair Powell’s vacated seat, which would allow for another nomination to Governor Miran’s seat. However, recent legal developments have complicated that path , at least in the near term . Following the DoJ’s subpoena of Chair Powell, Republican Senator Tillis pledged that the Senate Banking Committee will not move any Federal Reserve nominees forward for vote until the legal issue s are resolved. Tillis reiterated that vow this morning , even as he supported Warsh’s nomination . Other GOP senators have expressed concern about Fed independence more broadly as well . Moreover, while not our base case, these legal developments have increased the potential for Powell to stay on as a governor after his chair seat expires in May (see “Implications of the Fed’s latest legal developments” ). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 The effective tariff rate and high-frequency container traffic We continue to expect that the effective tariff rate will edge up to ~16.0% The Trump administration imposed additional tariffs on trading partners as of August 7 that pushed the effective tariff rate higher to 16.0%. Since then, negotiations with three of the US's largest trading partners – Mexico, Canada, and China – continue to proceed on a separate track. There have been recent announcements regarding both China and Canada. In addition, Section 232 reviews on trade in semiconductors, lumber, and pharmaceuticals, among others, remain ongoing. We expect that the effective tariff rate will remain around 15-16% in 2026. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on the legality of IEEPA tariffs in early November and we await a potential ruling, which could come any day that the court is in session. Given the calendar for the court and the lack of decision in January so far, if no decision is published on January 23, the earliest date for a decision to be released will be February 20. If IEEPA tariffs are invalidated, the effective tariff rate may move lower temporarily as the administration uses other trade authority to reconstitute its tariff regime. See here for more detailed views. Tariff receipts by the US Treasury continue to rise, with the rolling 63-day annualized customs and excise deposits at the Treasury at $380bn. records.text: 12 Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 China Xiaoqing Pi Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Helen Qiao Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Unravelling China's Investment downturn: (3) will AI replace property to drive FAI? China’s property downturn is now in its fifth year, with real‑estate investment down to roughly half its 2021 level and its share of total fixed-asset investment (FAI) falling to about 15% from the 25% peak. This implies a cumulative RMB6.5tn shortfall from peak to trough. At the same time, AI‑related FAI—data centers, power infrastructure, and high‑tech equipment—continues to accelerate on policy support and intensifying US – China tech competition, raising the question of whether the rising wave of AI capex can meaningfully cushion the drag from a prolonged property contraction. Complete report: Asia Economic Weekly: China: Will AI replace property to drive investment? 30 January 2026 AI capex remains too small to offset property for now In absolute terms, China’s current AI‑related FAI is still far too small to offset the property downturn. AI capex in 2025 is estimated at RMB 600–700bn (see AI Infrastructure - China (H/A): Powering up & cooling down for AIDC, 30 October 2025), or roughly 0.4–0.5% of GDP. This represents only a fraction of the expected RMB 8.3tn in property investment and roughly one‑third of the RMB 1.7tn contraction projected for the same year. This implies additional downward pressure on FAI in 2026–27, even if the drag begins to ease thereafter. I

As a result, AI‑driven investment in knowledge‑intensive services is likely to deliver the strongest productivity boost. However, large TFP gains do not automatically translate into rapid aggregate growth. Baumol’s cost disease remains a constraint: a large share of employment is concentrated in labor‑intensive services where output is harder to scale. When productivity rises in only part of the economy, economy‑wide wages tend to rise, pushing up costs elsewhere. In addition, AI may disrupt the labor market, as task automation tends to reduce labor’s share of income and increase capital’s share, especially where AI substitutes for human tasks at scale 2. Regulation, reform, and more flexible labor allocation In our view, the boost to potential growth will depend on how effectively workers displaced or redeployed by AI are matched to productive roles and sectors. In China’s case, well‑known hurdles to labor mobility and reallocation could limit how fully the economy captures productivity gains during this transition. More efficient reallocation will channel resources to higher‑productivity locations and sectors, and support GDP growth. As AI adoption spreads across services, we expect investment in the sector to rise over time. This view is based on the assessment that negative rates are not needed in light of the high rate differential to other major economies, and it is reinforced by the high hurdle for a further rate cut into negative territory that the SNB set after its last rate cut in June . The SNB appears confident about the expansionary effect of the current policy stance, both via the domestic economy and via the exchange rate. It detailed in the December meeting summary that the former is visible in the growth of money and credit aggregates (Figure 1M o n e y a n d c r e d i t g r o w t h ); the latter is visible in the overall stability of the exchange rate since April 2025, with the trade-weighted index gradually recovering after relatively short-lived bouts of risk- off driven appreciation (Figure 2N E E R a n d R E E R s i n c e J a n u a r y 2 0 2 5 ). All else equal, an expansionary policy stance should stimulate growth and inflation. The usual lags of monetary policy transmission mean this may not be visible in price and activity data yet but should nevertheless be working its way through the economy. records.text: Gold Mining30 January 2026 ab 6 Gold Mining UBS Research What's Priced In? This sounds like a simple question, but for the miners in our view it is not as it incorporates a view on valuation methodology/target multiple as well as the sensitivity of earnings to commodity prices. For the gold miners, we base our price targets on EV/ EBITDA but show what's priced using both target NTM EV/EBITDA multiples and NPV, and for each stock generate valuation sensitivities to a range of commodity prices and EV/EBITDA multiples. EV/EBITDA: To derive our EV/EBITDA-based implied prices we use 12-month forward multiples based on two-, five- and 10-year average 12-month forward consensus multiples. To determine what is priced in, we focus on 2yr/5yr multiple averages. Across our NA/EMEA gold coverage, we estimate on average equities are discounting ~$5,385/ oz using 5yrs average and ~$5,555/oz using 2yrs average multiple which is slightly below spot (~$5,340/oz). FNV, EDV, NEM and ABX are discounting the lowest price vs spot (below $5,200/oz), and KGC, HOC, and WPM are discounting the highest prices. NPV: On an NPV basis, we use a SoTP analysis using a consistent 6% WACC. We assume an 85x gold:silver price ratio, keep other by-products (copper/lead/zinc) and FX constant, and adjust the gold price to get to the current share price. records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 29 January 2026 Citi Research 15 been seen in Figure 23, where Citi’s commodity terms of trade indexes, have a high explanatory power for the moves year to date. We test a simple strategy where we go long commodity currencies when the CTOT is above its 55dma and vice versa. CLP , BRL, COP , ZAR, AUD, CAD, and NOK are used in this strategy, which uses a standard notional for each currency and is not risk adjusted. This strategy, shown in Figure 24, overall works reasonably well, resulting in an information ratio of 0.63. However, while the strategy recently performed well, it is still in a drawdown since early 2023. It seems to mostly work well when commodities are strongly trending, which has recently been the case. It would therefore likely take a continued strong trend in commodity prices to support this strategy going forward. We prefer to focus on the carry strategy, which is more consistently generating returns. However, there is an overlap between carry and commodity terms of trade currently, as many high carry names are also commodity producers, mostly in Latam. This makes it easier to stick with the carry theme at a time of strong commodities. Figure 23. Terms of trades were key driver of EMFX ytd Figure 24. records.text: The MPC is highly likely to hold Bank Rate at 3.75% at next week’s (5 February) n meeting given that recent communications have signalled caution around the pace of further cuts and the latest data have been mixed. We expect a 7-2 vote split – with Taylor and Dhingra preferring to lower Bank Rate – though risks are tilted towards more dissents. The near-term inflation projections should be revised down significantly given n the disinflationary impact of the Budget, with the updated numbers likely to show headline inflation falling to 2.1% in 2026Q2 and running close to target for the rest of the year. Further out in the forecast horizon, though, Budget measures are likely to slightly raise the inflation projection. Our analysis suggests that the Bank’s policy simulations will show a lower Bank n Rate path under two of the three policy rules and under the optimal policy projection given the notably lower near-term inflation forecast. That said, the policy path under the forward-looking Taylor rule – which Bailey had emphasised in November – could show marginally less easing than before, because this rule will look through the near-term forecast and instead respond to the medium-term inflation projection. We think that the guidance language will be largely unchanged, with the n Monetary Policy Summary indicating that Bank Rate remains on a gradual downward path but stressing that judgements around further policy easing will become a closer call. As a near-term driver, inflation forwards are likely to continue to pay more attention to volatile energy prices than FX moves, especially with tensions growing in the Middle East – Figure 3. The next move is still more likely a hike. While the ECB is likely to look through any energy-induced rise in inflation, the current upward pressure on inflation forwards reinforces the impression that the next move is still more likely to be an eventual hike. Indeed, we are positioned for such via Euribor U6/U8 steepeners (46bp as of 17:00 GMT 29Jan26. NB: Futures trading involves substantial risk of loss). One interesting development of late has been the de-coupling between market expectations for policy rates vs inflation – Figure 4. Since November, hike premium initially built as 1y1y inflation forwards fell, then the opposite has been the case more recently. This could just be noise, reflecting that relatively small changes are unlikely to jolt the ECB out of its stable policy baseline. However, the comments this week on the potential need for an ECB response should euro appreciation build could at least help to underline that the ECB does maintain full optionality and help to restore the sensitivity of policy rate vs inflation pricing. records.text: How to position? Banks and stocks with high free float That said, we don’t expect the $10bn in inflows to occur uniformly across the index as stocks with high free-float would see the largest increases in index weights from higher FOL changes. As a result, we view Banks as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for about three-fourths of the potential passive inflows, on our estimates. More broadly for the market, we favor positioning in names with true free float >49%, which would benefit most from a potential FOL change (also captured by GSXFSAFO). On the flip side, names with low true free float will likely benefit least from the FOL changes (also captured by GSXFSARO). In addition to the passive flows, given active funds maintain large underweights in Saudi Arabia, we see an opportunity for active funds to position in large liquid names with higher free float. Phased or delayed implementation are key risks We note that the upside from the FOL changes would be contained if regulatory authorities decide to implement a smaller increase to FOL, or if the decision gets pushed out. In the event that FOL increases are less than 100%, our estimates indicate $3bn-$9bn of passive flows based on the level of FOL increases (60-90%). In such a scenario, we believe the market reaction would be less positive per our macro model, but could be more negative given relatively wide anticipation of the announcement. records.text: 12 Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 China Xiaoqing Pi Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Helen Qiao Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Unravelling China's Investment downturn: (3) will AI replace property to drive FAI? China’s property downturn is now in its fifth year, with real‑estate investment down to roughly half its 2021 level and its share of total fixed-asset investment (FAI) falling to about 15% from the 25% peak. This implies a cumulative RMB6.5tn shortfall from peak to trough. At the same time, AI‑related FAI—data centers, power infrastructure, and high‑tech equipment—continues to accelerate on policy support and intensifying US – China tech competition, raising the question of whether the rising wave of AI capex can meaningfully cushion the drag from a prolonged property contraction. Complete report: Asia Economic Weekly: China: Will AI replace property to drive investment? 30 January 2026 AI capex remains too small to offset property for now In absolute terms, China’s current AI‑related FAI is still far too small to offset the property downturn. AI capex in 2025 is estimated at RMB 600–700bn (see AI Infrastructure - China (H/A): Powering up & cooling down for AIDC, 30 October 2025), or roughly 0.4–0.5% of GDP. This represents only a fraction of the expected RMB 8.3tn in property investment and roughly one‑third of the RMB 1.7tn contraction projected for the same year. This implies additional downward pressure on FAI in 2026–27, even if the drag begins to ease thereafter. I

records.text: European Rates Weekly 30 January 2026 Citi Research 12 Primary issuance in SSAs and covered bonds has started strong, as it usually does, but SSA supply has fallen slightly behind that of January 2025. Primary demand, on the other hand, has no signs of weakness as new € and $ deals attract higher- than-ever demand. Order book statistics show weaker bank treasury demand, offset by higher take-up by CB & OI, but this could be driven by higher WAM of YTD supply. Unsurprisingly, given the slightly slower supply and increased demand, € SSA and covered bond swap spreads continued to tighten in January. Supply: heavy as expected, but falling short of last year In SSAs, January primary issuance has been strong as it usually is, but YTD supply has fallen short of last year. As of 29 January, a total of €150bn equivalent has been issued in the main funding currencies (€, $ and £), €12bn or 7.6% less than last year. The YTD supply trends in € and $ that make the bulk of annual SSA supply, are at €78bn and $64bn 3.4% and 4.5% behind last year, respectively. Only Sterling SSA supply has gotten off to a better start than last year with £14.5bn issued YTD, 8.2% more than in January 2025. As of 29 January, SSA issuers completed 21% of the benchmark supply in the main funding currencies we expect from them in 2026, down from 23% last year. The YTD funding completion rate is the lowest for € SSAs at 17% with $ SSAs slightly ahead at 27%. Sterling SSA supply is off to a flying start with £14.5b

records.text: M Idea 12 Last Week in Review RBA February Preview – Decision Time (January 30, 2026): We think the RBA will hold rates in February, against market and consensus expectations. Inflation is above target but decelerating, with signs of slowing economic momentum emerging. Historically, the RBA has not chosen more active policy – if it does, it will drive weaker cyclical condition. Link: Australia Macro+: RBA February Preview: Decision Time (30 Jan 2026) 2026 February Reporting Season Calendar (January 28, 2026): This report covers companies under coverage in Australia that will be reporting interim and full-year results in February. Estimates for the respective reporting period are included, along with a brief comment from our analysts. Link: Australia Macro+: 2026 February Reporting Season Calendar (28 Jan 2026) 4Q CPI – Strong Headline, Better Detail (January 28, 2026): 4Q trimmed mean CPI came was in line with consensus at 0.9% QoQ (3.4% YoY), but above our estimate (and RBA Nov f/c) for 0.8% QoQ. Headline 0.6% QoQ, with annual rising to 3.8% YoY. ab 30 January 2026 Global Research Global Precious Metals Comment Higher gold as diversification intensifies We lift our gold price expectations We are raising our gold price forecasts to take into account stronger diversification flows amid Fed independence concerns, increased geopolitical tensions, and broader policy and political uncertainty, among other things. We now see prices averaging $5200 this year, with a year-end point target of $5600. The price changes we are making in gold move us from our previous base case to the upside scenario that we had flagged at the time, and imply further gains of ~12% from recent prices. Our new upside scenario sees gold averaging $5750 this year, which implies a test through $6000. Positive views are intact, the case for strategic allocations ever more compelling The flurry of headlines so far this year is intensifying investors’ desire to hold more diversified portfolios, with gold acting as a relative safe-haven asset to help protect against various possible macro outcomes. The lack of strong conviction on any potential scenario makes it challenging to also have strong conviction across the various asset classes. Gold stands out because it is one of the cleanest ways to position against US dollar weakness, broader concerns on fiat currencies, long-term worries about countries’ debt and fiscal deficits, lower real rates (either driven by sticky inflation and/or more dovish Fed), and potential policy missteps. records.text: ECB Preview—New Year , No Change The first ECB meeting of the year is likely to be uneventful, with the Governing Council leaving rates and all other policy parameters on hold. The main reason for this is that the incoming data have been broadly in line with the December staff projections. The preliminary flash estimate for Q4 GDP showed the Euro area growing 0.3%qoq (non-annualised), ahead of the staff projections of 0.2%. The details of the print looked somewhat firmer, given country-level evidence pointing to an improvement in domestic demand. Leading indicators for January were more mixed, with the PMIs and national surveys moving broadly sideways. Taken together, we left our forecast unchanged and continue to look for sequential growth of 0.3% in Q1 and 0.4% for the rest of the year, in line with the staff projections. The December inflation details have been consistent with the staff’s projections, with only a small miss for non-energy industrial goods at 0.5%yoy vs the ECB’s 0.6%. But we are tracking for a small downside surprise to the staff’s projections in January. At the time of writing, we forecast core inflation of 2.3%, which would leave our forecast for the Q1 average 0.2pp below the staff’s 2.4%. Other price indicators were mixed, as the increase in selling price expectations in the January flash PMIs was not corroborated by national surveys. Wait-and-see The February ECB meeting is likely to be uneventful. The press conference is likely to focus on the exchange rate, energy and questions about the next move. We doubt we will get anything new. ECB President Lagarde was particularly cautious and balanced back in December, despite hawkish forecasts giving her the opportunity to be otherwise. In this context, particular attention will be devoted to the implementation of the German fiscal package and defence-spending commitments across the euro area. In its December projections, Eurosystem staff estimated that new defence and infrastructure measures announced since March 2025 would add around 0.15pp per year to euro area real GDP growth in 2026 and 2027, and about 0.10pp in 2028. We see risks tilted towards a smaller growth impulse if the ramp-up in public investment crowds out private activity and/or if higher defence spending is met through increased imports from the US. In that context, it is notable that recent Bundesbank simulations point to only a modest boost to potential output from the German government's infrastructure plans – with estimated gains from 0.2 to 0.4pp by 2035 – and some simulations even suggesting that additional government investment can cause interest rates or wages to rise, thus crowding out private investment. The growing importance of domestic growth drivers must also be assessed against the backdrop of a an increasingly challenging external environment. The Nikkei and Yomiuri indicate growing momentum for the LDP , with Polymarket assigning a 74% probability of the LDP achieving a majority, up from 50% earlier in the week. If realised, initial market reactions may include equity gains, JPY depreciation, and higher JGB yields. However, these trends could reverse as markets assess the government’s limited ability to enact immediate fiscal expansion, such as a consumption tax cut, due to legislative constraints. New fiscal measures are unlikely to be presented before June, when longer plans on fiscal policies and growth strategies are finalised. Overall, we think the change in MBS allocation in the coming months will be closer or slightly larger than the 2.5% change implied by the model. We estimate that if spreads stay here, MBS overweights will decline by 2-3% in the coming months versus the 12.3% overweight at the end of December. Note that our approach suggests actual overweights will remain higher than our model output. Assuming $2-$2.5 trillion of AUM in active funds, this would translate to $45-$68bn of selling. We think more than half of this repositioning has already occurred and expect more to take place in the coming weeks if spreads stay here. We also show the sensitivity of the model overweights to spreads/spread changes in Figure 15. OAS would need to tighten a significant 34bp for the overweights to go to zero, all else being equal. Powell noted that core PCE inflation is likely to print at 3.0% y/y in December. Even if we exclude the tariff effect as a one-off, underlying inflation is above target. FOMC participants have argued that the tariffs have added 50-75bp to inflation. Our estimates are similar. Therefore, underlying inflation (ex of tariffs) is likely in the 2.25-2.5% range. And with fiscal policy turning notably easier this year, there is no clear impulse (other than lagged housing disinflation) for underlying inflation to move back to target. In turn, the real policy rate – which is what matters for the real economy – would be around 1.13-1.38%. This is close to, or lower than, six-to-nine participants’ implied longer run projections of the real rate (r*, i.e., their dot plot projections minus 2%). And it’s within touching distance of the longer run median real rate (1%). records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW By expanding our BNP Paribas US and eurozone Financial Conditions Indices, we aim to provide an easy-to-interpret summary of market-based measures that track and quantify the degree of looseness or tightness of financing conditions facing investors and the real economy in each new country covered. We now incorporate: United Kingdom, Norway, Sweden, Japan, Switzerland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. We still express financial conditions as z-scores, using a two-layer approach. We first express our components – bonds, credit spreads, equities, FX, volatility and, in some cases, commodities – as z-scores. We, then, combine them into a final aggregated index that is standardised once again through z-scoring. For a full explanation, please see New BNP Paribas Financial Conditions Index: Growth drop-off in H2 dated 5 March 2023 and BNP Paribas EZ Financial Conditions Index: Growth at a standstill dated 28 November 2023. There are two main differences between this methodology and that applied in our US and eurozone FCIs, however, as we explain on pages 3 and 4. The new G10 Financial Conditions Indices will also be published daily on Bloomberg. In addition, users can follow the contribution charts and obtain more details through a weekly chartbook publication in our Quant Vault. The BoE's reaction function is very important – in the near term, it is key to its actions. But the fundamentals of the economy determine the medium-term rate path. If we are right about the aforementioned judgments, we think that the terminal rate could fall to 3%, with cuts in March, July and November. A faster global growth uptick than projected by Morgan Stanley, as well as a sharp change in fiscal policy direction in the UK, remain key risks to that view. Despite missing the government's ambitious 2025 investment and defense spending targets, the fiscal regime shift is becoming increasingly apparent in the federal budget data. Total federal expenditures increased by over 10% in 2025. n A stronger federal spending momentum towards the end of the year. While both defense and investment expenditures saw a significant pick-up after the end of preliminary budgeting mode in September, this acceleration in Q4 was insufficient to meet the annual spending targets due to the limited time available. However, these dynamics indicate an increased spending pace in 2026. n Non-financial spending hurdles remain the key challenge. Achieving the even more ambitious investment and defense spending targets for 2026 will likely prove challenging for the government. Excluding real estate and infrastructure, services‑sector FAI slowed sharply in 2H25. The weakness likely reflects sluggish consumption and fragile consumer confidence. As we wrote last week (see “Fed Notes: What Warsh could mean for the Fed ”), Warsh has a strong pedigree, with a background somewhat similar to Chair Powell – a lawyer by training, not a PhD economist, who has had an impressive mix of experience in the public and private sectors. In terms of policy, Warsh has noted that the Fed could bring down inflation by reducing the size of its balance sheet, which in turn could allow for lower policy rates. A sharp weakening in the USD, absent a weakening in the economy, as has happened year to date (see here), is more likely to result in higher inflation risk premium and thus higher nominal term premium. Figure 8 shows that unlike in Q1 25 when both inflation breakevens and the USD were weakening, this time around inflation breakevens have widened. The difference being that back in 2025, the market was gearing up for a negative growth shock as tariff-related policy uncertainty was rising. Indeed, even though the left coalition has agreed to conduct its primaries to elect their candidate in October, heavyweights like Melenchon and Glucksmann have refused to participate. For now, markets have chosen to ignore the fiscal risk that is still present. The proposed deficit target of 5% of GDP in the budget is likely only the floor, and a realization of the current commitment to the EC to reach 3% deficit by 2029 looks ambitious. The market is likely to be comfortable with this level of OAT spreads only as long as vol is low and carry is the main EGB theme. This is the reverse of PGBs, which are struggling to outperform even though they remain cheap to fundamentals at a flat spread to Bonos, in our view. records.text: M Idea 2 Finishing on a strong note, but with a conundrum Durable goods orders continue to move higher... November durable goods orders rose 5.3% m/m, a touch above our expectation (MS: 5.0% m/m), and are now up 12.3% from a year earlier (note: durable goods orders are presented in current dollars). Nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft (core durable goods orders) grew 0.7%, the fifth consecutive monthly gain. This series is a closely watched proxy for business spending plans. Both orders and shipments of this component have been on a consistent uptrend. Furthermore, growth in orders has moved in line with shipments for the past year and a half, following a period when orders persistently undershooting shipments ( Exhibit 1 ). Not surprising from our perspective is the robust upward momentum in orders of computers and related products, which rose 20.5% y/y through November, while shipments are up by a solid 14.4%. These orders include computers, computer storage devices and other peripheral computer equipment. However, this category is a small weight in orders of durable goods. Domestic production of computers and related products is small, certainly from a historical perspective. Most computer and peripherals are now imported. Elsewhere, we see an AI echo in orders of electrical equipment, appliance, and components. This subsector manufactures products that generate, distribute and use electrical power. Euro Area Economics I The European economy and equities are not the same. In economics, a 5% EUR appreciation, in effective terms (i.e. trade weighted - broadly equivalent to 10% EUR/USD), reduces euro area exports by 1.5% and growth by 0.3pp, with France, Italy and Spain's economic growth most sensitive, on our estimates. It is worth noting here that there is in general a 2:1 ratio between the moves in EUR/USD and those of euro in nominal effective terms. Inflation channels differ and centre on oil (which is priced in USD) and final and intermediate imported goods (which comes through slowly). Taken together, we estimate a 10% EUR/USD appreciation lowers euro area inflation by 30bp. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS The curious case of the US dollar The weakness of the US dollar is in vogue these days, but we think part of the narrative is overblown. US exceptionalism has allowed sustained current account and fiscal deficits to be easily financed at low interest rates while leading to a historically strong dollar as capital flowed to the US. Despite uncertainty and policy changes, the relative outperformance of the US shows no signs of cracking. True, the dollar may have lost some of its luster, including its hedging properties, and some further depreciation may follow. But there are limits to how much depreciation could take place, not least because monetary policy abroad would react to it. And if the story is about fiscal profligacy and dollar (and other currencies’) debasement, then we should be asking ourselves how much more room to run real assets may have. Morgan Commodities Research, Rystad, EIA Winter freeze-offs: impact on demand Periods of sharp winter cooling tend to refocus market attention on the power sector, as peak electricity demand coincides with heightened volatility across fuel prices. During such episodes, the relative economics and physical availability of different generation sources can shift rapidly, occasionally triggering short-term fuel switching—most commonly from gas to coal or oil— as systems attempt to preserve reliability during periods of stress. Despite this seasonal sensitivity, oil and oil products play only a marginal role in global electricity generation. In 2024, oil accounted for less than 2% of total global power output, compared with coal at 34% and natural gas at 22%, which together remain the dominant sources of dispatchable generation worldwide (Figures 5 & 6). Global electricity generation from oil has declined structurally over the past decade. After peaking at around 1,150 TWh in 2012, oil-fired generation fell to 763 TWh by 2018 and declined further to below 700 TWh in 2024. records.text: Japan Macro Watch30 January 2026 ab 3 Beyond April, we are expecting a rise in service (and some goods) inflation as firms likely pass through higher labor costs to their prices at the beginning of the new fiscal year. We observe that inflation expectations of corporates and households are rising in the survey (Figure 3), and our base scenario anticipates the gradual uptrend in inflation expectations would continue even if CPI inflation slows in the coming months. The rise in inflation expectations, coupled with above-potential growth (1% real GDP growth vs. potential growth rate of 0.6-0.7%), should theoretically act as a force to sustain higher inflation. However, we have reservations about this view. We are confident that large corporate inflation expectations have firmly risen. However, the inflation expectations of consumers/households and small firms may be vulnerable. The fact that all national political parties except one are proposing consumption tax cuts could be evidence that people are not accepting inflation. With a lack of labor strikes to demand higher wages and salaries despite complaints about a fall in real income, we sense that the inertia of a deflationary mindset remains strong. In other words, we see little risk of a sharp rise in inflation expectations, and the recent acceleration in breakeven inflation expectations in the rates market may be overly exaggerated. records.text: 29 January 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 14 Uncertainty criteria “Requires that uncertainty about future inflation increases less than linearly with the forecast horizon” – John Williams For our analysis of the uncertainty criteria, we focus on how the variance of inflation expectations (a measure of uncertainty) changes with the forecast horizon. The basic framework for this criterion is to use the variance of inflation expectations at the short- and medium-term to form a linear prediction of inflation expectation at a longer-term and then see if the actual variance of long -term inflation expectations is below that prediction (which would imply a “ less than linear” increase in variance/uncertainty). Our formal analysis is restricted to just SPF professional expectations. While it is possible to use market data to derive an option ‑implied risk ‑neutral distribution inflation, risk‑neutral probabilities may differ significantly from physical, or true, probabilities and thus be misleading. In addition, liquidity in the EUR inflation options market has become extremely poor which will hamper estimates. The dbDataInsights only asks questions about short -term (1 year) and long -term (5- 10 year) inflation expectations, meaning we do not have expectations for enough short-to-medium-term horizons to form a linear prediction for long -term expectations. records.text: US Rates Weekly 30 January 2026 Citi Research 8 Short-end: Balance sheet dynamics Warsh and the outlook for Fed balance sheet Kevin Warsh will likely be nominated to succeed Jerome Powell as chair of the Federal Reserve. Warsh strongly favors a smaller Fed balance sheet; just a couple months ago he called it “bloated” and argued it “can be reduced significantly. That largesse can be redeployed in the form of lower interest rates to support households and small and medium-size businesses” , in a WSJ op-ed. Warsh has long held these views; for example, in a 2010 speech he argued that “as the Fed's balance sheet expands, it becomes more of a price maker than a price taker in the Treasury market” , adding that “if the Fed's holdings work predominantly through the so-called portfolio balance channel, the cessation of purchases should not reverse any benefits attained”. Market pricing for H2 SOFR/FF basis, including U6 and Z6, moved 0.5bp lower today, likely on the back of the Warsh headlines. In our view, a Warsh-led Fed could potentially reduce RMPs to the lower end of the range, stop RMPs altogether, or even restart QT. The latter of the three outcomes is the least likely one, but it seems that markets are underpricing the risk of such an outcome. With SRP now uncapped, the Fed could eventually seek to transition to a reserves framework closer to that of the BoE. BoJ policy outlook and alternative view on JPY Currently, the OIS market is pricing in a 65% probability of the BoJ's next policy rate hike from the current 0.75% to 1.0% on April 28. We maintain our BoJ call, which anticipates the next hike in June (a semiannual gradual rate hike). In our view, the primary reason the market is pricing in an April hike is the threat of further JPY depreciation. We share the view that the JPY is a critical determinant of the BoJ's policy reaction, and the government likely perceives JPY depreciation as harmful, even though a weak JPY level is necessary for the "high pressure economy" policy. Indeed, the last three rate hikes occurred following notable JPY depreciation (Figure 4). Therefore, we argue that the risk is skewed toward an earlier rate hike in April rather than a later one as our base case expects JPY to remain weak. However, we see the possibility that the currency market (and bond market) may reverse the trend (JPY depreciation and JGB yields rising) in the coming weeks and months. As stated above, we think that the sharp rise in breakeven inflation expectations could be too exaggerated, which may decline soon. This implies that real yields could rise, and that could be a reason for JPY appreciation. Even if fiscal anxieties rise post election, we see limited incentive for a wholesale shift back to domestic credit, given local supply constraints and unattractive relative valuations. 9. Why Has Year to Date Credit Issuance Been Absorbed So Well? Strong January issuance absorption reflects typical seasonal strength, reset expectations in Q4, and pre-positioning via selling higher beta credit and raising cash into year end. While consensus expects $1.8–1.9T of 2026 IG supply (above our $1.725T forecast), issuance has historically had no statistical significance in spread fair value models. Fund beta and cash metrics show managers boosted liquidity into late 2025, particularly in HY/LL, creating dry powder for new deal uptake. 10. Should Investors Worry About Rising M&A and Large LBO/LL Deals? The picture is mixed. Leveraged loan markets have seen a clear pickup: lower rated and non refi LL supply stands at 17% and 70%, respectively, near the 75th and 55th percentiles—worthy of attention. In contrast, HY issuance remains more benign: lower rated and non refi HY volumes sit below averages at near 13% and 33%. These figures will rise given the current pipeline, but the overall signal is that while some credit conditions appear loose, it is not systemwide yet.

records.text: 29 January 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 Introduction The European Central Bank (ECB) is navigating a complex monetary landscape. While inflation is set to undershoot the 2% target over the course of this year, the medium-term outlook points to stronger inflationary pressures. The key question for investors in the short -term is whether the ECB will "look through" this temporary dip and hold rates steady, or if they will take a further insurance cut. The stability of inflation expectations will be one of the key contributors to the ECB’s policy decision this year . In this report, we assess how securely these expectations are anchored as the ECB faces inflation persisting below target for a while. The forthcoming inflation undershoot 2026 is set to be the year of the inflation undershoot. We expect that the euro area flash HICP prints released next Wednesday (4 February) will confirm that headline inflation has fallen from 1.9% (YoY) in December to 1.65% in January, the lowest level since April 2021 . Energy base effects are a large driver of this decline and should help keep inflation below target throughout 2026. But core goods inflation is also historically low. Gradually these effects will fade, and inflation should return toward target. Balance risks ahead We continue to view risks around the forward rate path as broadly balanced. While the probability of further cuts has diminished, rate hikes also remain unlikely. With (1) inflation projected to remain well below target through 2026, (2) limited signs of high‑inflationary pressure emerging in 2027, and (3) supportive SEK dynamics, we doubt the Riksbank will feel compelled to tighten policy. Even a stronger economic recovery would be unlikely to trigger early hikes, given how far the economy is from any kind of “overheating” scenario. records.text: US Rates Weekly 30 January 2026 Citi Research 15 Interestingly, the market is pricing for more movement in rates but not in the curve given that the implied swaption vol is currently trading well above the realized rate vol while the implied CMS curve vol is trading essentially on top on the realized curve vol (Figure 26). Even though implied/realized vol ratios historically have not been good leading indicators for vol, we believe the divergence between the two measures highlights the currently different risk profiles between the two option instruments. For vanilla swaptions, the elevated risk premium should continue to attract carry hungry vol sellers, which in turn will likely keep short-dated implied vol contained in the near term. In contrast, curve options’ low risk premium in an already low vol environment suggests that they are undervalued as tail hedges. The relative cheapness of 30s/2s CMS curve option is also reflected in the implied correlation, which has remained elevated and unchanged despite the sharp decline in the realized correlation (Figure 27). Typically, the implied correlation is expected to trade below the realized correlation to reflect the premium embedded in the CMS curve options, but that does not have to be the case if the market is expecting the decorrelated rates behavior to be short-lived. This could of course be the case because when risk aversion rises, typically USDJPY moves lower and risky assets like EMFX do poorly. Given that risk aversion is not rising in line with the USDJPY move, this correlation may not be operational right now. However, even if we just focus on periods where a stronger JPY is driven by intervention (and not just by risk aversion), still suggests downside for EMFX, as can be seen in Figure 5. This is clearly somewhat worrying for our EM carry basket. However, we seem to be in a generalized weak USD environment, and EMFX did well with a rising JPY, and gave back some of these gains on the following weak JPY day. We are therefore hesitant to give up on our carry basket, before we get a clearer sense of volatility picking up. For now, the move up in volatility has not reached levels that trigger caution, as per Figure 6, at least when abstracting from OVX, which is the least concerning volatility indicator. Ending this measure could lead to higher prices for domestic chemical products, significantly impacting a wide range of industries and people’s lives. That said, preferential treatment for naphtha, a fossil fuel, runs counter to the global trend toward decarbonization. The consistency of these measures should also be considered. We build on a prior note to discuss what this nomination could mean for the Fed. Warsh’s background Warsh has a strong pedigree to be chair of the Federal Reserve, with a background somewhat similar to Chair Powell. Warsh is a lawyer by training, not a PhD economist, who has had an impressive mix of experience in the public and private sectors. On the public side, Warsh was a governor at the Federal Reserve from 2006 through 2011, a period that spanned the Fed’s response to the GFC. During that period, he served as an important liaison between the Fed and markets. On the private side, Warsh has held various roles, including currently as a partner at Stan Druckenmiller’s family office, Duquesne. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 9 Core views Growth: a dose of optimism • Our 2026 average US GDP growth forecast of 2.8% is well above consensus (2.1%). The key drivers are easier fiscal and monetary policy, and our expectation of more growth-friendly trade policy. We now project that consumer stimulus from the OBBBA will be more front-loaded into tax season. This prompts us to tweak our forecasts: we modestly raise 1H 2026 growth and lower 2H. Risks to our projections are tilted to the upside. A 3-handle on 2026 growth wouldn’t be a big surprise. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We continue to expect inflation to remain above the Fed's target throughout our forecast horizon. In the near term, supply-driven inflation due to tariffs should push inflation above 3% y/y through 3Q 2026 as businesses continue to slowly shift costs to consumers. Inflationary pressures from tariffs should fade towards the end of 2026; however, core PCE inflation should end 2026 at an elevated 2.9% y/y and only decline to 2.4% by year end 2027. We continue to believe underlying inflation is above 2%, and our growth and monetary policy outlook should generate more demand driven inflation causing a delay in inflation’s return to the Fed’s 2% target. FIGURE 2. ... as reserves were much lower Source: Federal Reserve, Barclays Research Source: Federal Reserve, Barclays Research Reserves are currently around $2.9tn; why do banks hold so much in reserves? Banks use reserves to settle payment flows as well as to maintain appropriate liquidity buffers such as holding enough liquid assets to fund outflows under liquidity requirements such as the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) as well as lowering net stable funding requirements. Fedwire funds service settles $4.5tn in payments on average each day, but there is no netting of this flow. That means if banks have large payment needs and lower reserve balances, they need to overdraw their reserve account to potentially settle these. The Fed issues banks credit to do this and to keep the payment system flowing, otherwise the gross settlements over Fedwire might seize up in a system with lower reserves. Since the Fed has operated with a large balance sheet, however, overdrafts have been negligible. For instance, prior to the GFC, the Fed’s balance sheet would increase up to twenty-fold intraday, as it extended credit to banks even on an unsecured basis. This created credit risks to the Fed, and in a sense the end-of-day snapshot of a small Fed balance sheet was largely a mirage. These criteria are tested against a diverse set of inflation expectations data, including household surveys from the ECB and Deutsche Bank, the ECB's Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF), and market -implied expectations. Our results reveal a significant divergence between economic agents. Expectations from professional forecasters and financial markets appear well - anchored, showing low sensitivity to recent shocks and levels consistent with the ECB's target. In contrast, h ousehold expectations show more ambiguity and fragility. Overall, our findings suggest that inflation expectations are not currently de - anchored. The stability observed among professionals should give the ECB the confidence to 'look through' the temporary inflation undershoot and hold its policy steady. However, the fragility of household expectations warrants close monitoring, as this group repres ents the most likely source of a potential de - anchoring. Should a significant economic shock occur, or the inflation undershoot prove deeper than forecast, such a de -anchoring would raise the probability of further easing for precautionary or insurance purposes. records.text: M Idea 8 Reverting back to pay surveys, we see a high likelihood that in the more normal labour market conditions, they might not be as useful as in 2022 and 2023. However, we wonder whether the DMP survey at, say, 3.6% as opposed to 3.3% really allows for extrapolations as significant as those around the UK's NAIRU? Spot ex-bonus private sector AWE growth is at 3.6% 3M/Y as of November, and likely to undershoot last year's DMP estimate for 3.9% 3M/Y pay growth in 4Q25. Finally, we note that the BoE has not yet commented on the UK's recent spell of more robust productivity growth. On our estimates, productivity growth in the UK is running at 2%Y in the private sector as of 3Q25. Should such momentum be sustained, pay growth in excess of 3.5% would be perfectly target-consistent, especially given the likely subdued import price pressures over 2026; those in any case are running at ~1%Y in 2H25. First, this is only an approximation of the BoE’s model, and there is limited scope to validate how well it replicates the Bank’s results outside of the paths published in the November MPR. Second, the results naturally depend on the central projection, and so if this differs from our expectation then the paths would also differ. Agents’ Pay Survey Likely to Come in Close to Preliminary Expectations The December minutes noted that a key input into the MPC’s thinking at this meeting would be the Agents’ annual survey of firms’ expectations for pay settlements. Our analysis suggests that settlements are likely to average 3.4% this year, down from 3.9% in 2025, and we expect the survey be roughly in line with that figure. While our forecast is higher than the pre-pandemic average, it is close to the Agents’ preliminary estimate of 3½% and so would not represent a significant surprise relative to the Bank’s expectations. We also think that our estimate is consistent with wage growth normalisation this year because average weekly earnings growth tends to run below average settlements when the labour market is loose. Guidance Likely to be Largely Unchanged The guidance language will likely be broadly unchanged, with the Monetary Policy Summary indicating that Bank Rate remains on a gradual downward path but emphasising that judgements around further policy easing will become a closer call. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley MUFG 3 Exhibit 1: Policy Board Members’ Majority Outlook for FY2025-27 Source: Bank of Japan, Morgan Stanley Research Thus far, the BoJ has explained that “as cost-push factors wane, realized inflation will fall below 2% going forward.” That explanation has been maintained this time as well. Because the government’s large-scale price-suppression measures will exert a near-term downward effect, headline inflation may temporarily decline. If, despite fully incorporating the government’s suppression measures, the BoJ has still materially revised up its underlying inflation outlook, it could have plausibly explained this as inflation proving more persistent than expected, due to changes in firms’ price-setting behavior, among other factors. Our impression is that the BoJ used the government measures’ downward effect to raise its outlook in a less conspicuous manner; in any case, when the latest projections are assessed after accounting for the government’s price- suppression measures, they suggest the BoJ’s conviction in achieving its price stability target has strengthened further than before. In that sense, the BoJ appears to be shifting away from its prior stance of “inflation will fall, so there is no need to rush rate hikes.” The market is also pricing the BoJ’s post- January meeting pace of hikes at roughly once every six months. Source: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas The KOSPI 200 and Taiex have outperformed US peers YTD Taking a breather: South Korea’s KOSPI 200 (+26.3%) and Taiwan’s Taiex (+12.3%) have been two of the best performing indices in APAC equities year-to-date – and have outperformed the Nasdaq 100 (+2.5%) and the Magnificent 7 (+0.9%) by a significant margin. We believe one of the main drivers for the performance divergence is the sentiment shift between hardware and software. While prices for memory and storage chips have risen sharply in recent months due to severe supply–demand imbalances, software companies have faced downward price pressure from advanced AI coding capabilities and intensifying competition among leading AI models. In addition, the introduction of new AI chip systems and the rising popularity of custom TPUs are boosting growth expectations for foundry companies and AI server makers in Taiwan. Major companies in the memory, storage, and foundry sectors across South Korea and Taiwan have released quarterly earnings over the past two weeks, which we believe gives investors a chance to carefully evaluate the sustainability of the sharp rise in tech hardware pricing and the related AI capex. January freeze-offs: impact on supply The Arctic cold wave that swept across the US on January 25–26 triggered widespread freeze-offs in key producing regions. We estimate production fell from roughly 6.6 mbd on January 21 to around 5.0 mbd at the trough, based on daily gas scrapes, implying a peak decline of 1.6 mbd. In this sense, it was a very strategic use of rate checks. Q7: How does the US intervene in forex market? Decisions on US currency policy are in general made by the Treasury Department. When there is intervention, orders are normally executed by the NY Fed. The US Treasury Department uses the Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF) to intervene, and the Fed will normally intervene to the same amount via the SOMA. As of November 2015, the ESF asset balance was $216.5bn, with ¥172.9bn (around 80%) in special drawing rights (SDRs) provided by the IMF. The ESF holds only $20.1bn in US Treasuries. Occasionally we hear some say that if the US participates in forex intervention funding for USD buying can expand with no limit, but this is fundamentally mistaken. If the US is to provide quantitative support for Japanese intervention to buy the JPY, it would be more effective for Fed to increase USD selling via the SOMA or to provide USD funding via currency swaps with the BoJ. However, even if the US Treasury Department were to make such a request we do not think the Fed would agree to it, so this is not a realistic option. Another possibility would be to convert a part of EUR assets held by the ESF (around $13.0bn) to JPY assets (around $6.0bn). Bruna Skarica Central forecast: We assume that the BoE staff will shift the unemployment rate forecast up by 20bp, marking to market, and embedding a jobless rate peak of 5.3% in 2Q26. Similarly, we think that taking into account 2H25 hard data will push the 2025 and 2026 growth forecasts lower, to 1.4%Y and 1.1%Y, from 1.5%Y and 1.2%Y, respectively. A higher jobless rate means more slack. We expect the output gap forecast to show an average widening of ~20bp in excess supply throughout the forecast horizon. We see the risks around these estimates as balanced. The staff's tone on the labour market in the December meeting minutes was notably more bearish, so there is some chance that the peak in the jobless rate is lifted to above 5.3%, with the anticipated employment growth uptick potentially dulled down. The BoE would, thus, implicitly acknowledge that the UK's productivity outlook might be improving a bit more than what has been embedded in the November forecasts. On the other hand, the staff have previously surprised us with their bearishness on the UK's supply capacity, so we don't discount that this happens again. We expect wage growth in 2027 and 2028 to be taken down a notch on the back of a bit more slack and lower 2026 inflation. Scenario 2: The ruling coalition fails to win a majority – A predictable "storm," followed by an uncertain voyage This scenario would first bring about a "change of leader according to the rules." Prime Minister Takaichi would likely take responsibility for the defeat and resign, and the LDP would plunge into a leadership election. Even if the prime minister were to try to stay on, she would be held accountable for having called an election, even delaying budget deliberations, for this result. This instability is predictable. The problem, however, lies beyond that. Just because the ruling coalition loses its majority does not mean an immediate "change of government" to the opposition. Instead, Japan would enter an extremely opaque negotiation period over the very "framework of government" itself. Two conceivable paths are: 1) the formation of an opposition-led government; and 2) the LDP maintaining power by finding a new coalition partner. Which path is taken is completely unpredictable. The market would watch this entire negotiation process with bated breath. The initial market reaction after the election would likely be a reversal of the "Takaichi trade," i.e., lower stocks, a stronger yen, and a flatter yield curve. records.text: d balance sheet was largely a mirage. In contrast, daylight overdrafts are quite low now as a share of reserve balances, meaning banks have enough liquidity to settle payments flow without borrowing from the Fed. This system design strikes us as much more logical: banks hold more liquidity, intraday credit from the Fed is lower. It is no wonder that the Fed landed on this "ample" framework rather than going back to the era of scarce reserves. We think there would be very little support on the committee to move away from ample and back to scarce. So what might change on balance sheet policy? There is a bit of wiggle room within what the Fed defines as ample. What it means in practice is likely on the order of a few hundred billion in reserves. We talked about two camps at the Fed already, those that want enough reserves in the system all the time to accommodate even the largest swings in the TGA, and those that prefer a smaller balance sheet most of the time, with the Fed’s repo backstop facility (SRP) providing marginal reserves when those larger swings occur. A Fed chair that is aiming for a smaller balance sheet might find support for doing fewer reserve management purchases (RMPs) over time, and running repo pressures a touch higher at times, to achieve a lower balance sheet, which would be well within the bounds of the Fed’s existing framework. records.text: ab 30 January 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives SNB outlook: Where could we be wrong? How robust is our expectation for unchanged SNB policy rates in 2026? Since the December SNB meeting the CHF has strengthened by c.2% in nominal effective terms to new all-time highs. This renewed CHF appreciation amid geopolitical risks and broader USD weakness has drawn attention and reignited the discussion about SNB FX intervention and/or the risk for negative policy rates. Our baseline view, which we confirm today, remains an unchanged policy rate at 0% in 2026 and discretionary FX interventions as first line of defence against CHF strength. This view is based on the SNB's assessment that the policy stance is already expansionary and negative rates are not needed in light of the elevated rate differential to other major economies. It is reinforced by the high hurdle for a further rate cut into negative territory that the SNB set after its last rate cut in June. Market pricing of just 5bp of cuts this year also appears to give credence to the SNB’s line of communication from June. That said, we acknowledge that the central bank has a certain history of surprising markets. We therefore outline our thinking on alternative scenarios to the SNB outlook and the likelihood of negative rates. What is perhaps most interesting is the decoupling between the dollar and US interest rates. In our view, this reflects that the dollar may have lost some of its hedging appeal, as it has not performed as a safe haven in the event of US-specific policy risks. In other words, the decoupling between the dollar and US interest rates could be a sign of US- specific risk premium. The limits to real dollar depreciation Despite the decoupling between the dollar and interest rates, and the dollar’s slide in the past year, there are limits to how much real dollar depreciation can be. Even after the recent dollar depreciation and the further move we may expect, the dollar remains about equally strong in real terms as three years ago (Exhibit 3). So what are the limits we have in mind? A large real depreciation of the dollar vis-à-vis other currencies would be a recessionary shock for the global economy ex-US. And while some economies with strong momentum could withstand it well, most developed economies would not emerge unscathed. Wait-and-see The February ECB meeting is likely to be uneventful. The updated assessment should “reconfirm that inflation should stabilise at the 2% target in the medium term.” That would pave the way for no change in policy rates and only fine-tuning of communication. They will reiterate that the ECB will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach. Uncertainty will be in focus, which can be perceived as marginally dovish. The press conference is likely to focus on the exchange rate, energy and questions about the next move. We doubt we will get anything new. ECB President Lagarde was particularly cautious and balanced back in December, despite hawkish forecasts giving her the opportunity to be otherwise. We doubt she will deviate from that caution next week. If uncertainty was a key factor back then for Lagarde to remain prudent, it has only increased since. Several clients have asked questions on whether investors could replicate MBS-like exposure through a combination of linear rate instruments such as Treasuries and non-linear ones such as swaptions. In this piece, we show some examples of the construction of such strategies. That said, we do not think that the MBS market is the main driver of the fall in implied vol. Rather, factors like low close-to-close realized vol (this was among the lowest realized vol months for 10y rates in decades, Figure 4), very anchored views about the Fed (on hold, with low probabilities of hikes or significant cuts), and the Treasury's reliance on bills for funding are likely driving vol lower. We also think that seasonal vol supply from callables has pushed intermediate vols lower and think that this factor will fade over the next few months. How are rate market instruments used to create MBS-like payoffs? MBS are long duration, short convexity and short vega (sensitivity to interest rate implied volatility) instruments, in addition to offering an OAS if one theoretically hedges out these risks. The OAS is compensation for the fact that that prepayment behavior is not perfectly predictable. This means that a combination of a linear rates instrument and a rate vol instrument can be used to create an MBS-like exposure, subject to basis risk. 29 January 2026 27 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Sleepy, no more

As usual in such situation, the challenge will be not to get carried away when the better data comes in. So far, we still think we are still in the rather shallow stage of improvement : German ZEW improved, but the Ifo didn’t, The Euro area composite PMI moved sideways. The European Commission Sentiment Indicator, which we prefer, improved more meaningfully across components. It’s the third time since May 2025 that consumer, industry, services, retail, construction and employment indicators improved simultaneously, after four years where that happened only once. There isn’t much to lament about in the survey, except perhaps that consumers’ savings intentions have risen, and that’s pivotal for domestic growth, and that in spite of improving manufacturing sentiment, quarterly surveys still show a decline in capacity utilisation. More hidden, lending dynamics are getting better, especially in the >5y maturities to corporates, but that’s not news and not accelerating. And, uncertainty is higher again than in late-2025, the EUR is stronger, and energy price increases are never usually particularly good news for sentiment.

records.text: US Economics 30 January 2026 Citi Research 2 Modest job growth but a decline in the unemployment rate in December helped ease some concerns of an imminent further weaking in the labor market after the unemployment rate had consistently climbed through the second half of 2025. January data could further reinforce the perception of stability in the labor market, with solid 135k jobs added and the unemployment rate unchanged at 4.4% in our forecast. But we would caution that January is still within the time of year that seasonal adjustment is particularly favorable for employment data. As in previous years, initial and continuing jobless claims have also been lower in recent weeks around the holiday season/start of the new year. It may be misleading to extrapolate stronger January data to future months and conclude that the labor market is durably stabilizing. Strong residual seasonality also means that a potential downside surprise to January employment data could be a more meaningful signal for the health of the labor market. Some data that have shown residual January strength in the past have not been as favorable in early 2026 readings, such as the Conference Board’s labor market differential. Benchmark revisions released with January figures should also show much lower employment in 2025, likely by around 700k, complicating the market reaction to the data. Overall, we do not expect that January employment data will significantly change our view that the labor market will co

ar residual seasonal pattern in jobs data since 2023. Benchmarking employment to official data should substantially lower the level of employment as of March 2025. Preliminary benchmark estimates implied around 900k fewer jobs, but final estimates will likely be smaller, possibly around -700k. While months after March will not be benchmarked, QCEW data so far for Q2 suggest monthly payroll employment continues to overstate true job growth, at least by the ~60k/month estimated by Chair Powell. One source of uncertainty with the January jobs report will be an update to birth/death model adjustments. This could imply downside risks to monthly employment figures as the updated B/D model is intended to bring monthly payroll estimates closer to “true” employment levels that have been consistently lower. The BLS briefly incorporated these new model adjustments in data from April 2024 to October 2024. The B/D adjustments in these months were about 50k lower than ones used in the previous year. This resulted in January carry being the most negative in several years ( Figure 6). While officially there is no way to see November 2025 NSA m/m, mechanically (since the TIPS market used the fallback of 325.604 for October) carry is behaving as if it were -0.46% m/m. How large would the impact on the economy and national finances (SNA basis, excluding regional finances) be if the consumption tax rate on food items (those currently subject to the reduced 8% rate) were lowered to 0%? The annual tax reduction would be JPY4.8trn, of which JPY3.7trn corresponds to the national tax portion. In addition, because 19.5% of consumption tax revenue is allocated to local allocation tax grants, the tax cut would reduce these grants by JPY0.7trn, resulting in a net JPY3trn deterioration in the primary balance (PB) as a direct national impact. Consumption tax cuts also affect GDP . By lowering tax-inclusive prices, they are expected to shift consumption from the pre-cut and post-cut periods into the tax-cut period and stimulate spending by reducing the economic burden on households, thereby boosting real GDP . However, using multipliers from the Cabinet Office’s macroeconomic model (2022 edition), the decline in the GDP deflator caused by lower tax-inclusive prices more than offsets the increase in real GDP , lowering nominal GDP . Moreover, because food is a necessity with low price elasticity, the real GDP-boosting effect would likely be more limited than for a broad-based tax cut. First, we examine how changes in average inflation expectations move in response to various measures of macroeconomic data surprises. Second, we examine how the expectations of individuals respond to inflation shocks. Sensitivity to macro data surprises – Covariance analysis It is difficult to measure “economic shocks” or to know which shocks are most relevant. All measures have some form of smoothing applied to them. This smoothing is not ideal for our analysis as we will not be comparing the change in inflation expectations to the surprise that has occurred in the same period, but rather to the surprise that has occurred over the last few periods. And yet, the effectiveness of the current policy stance is the most frequently debated point in our client conversations. In our experience, market participants observe developments in precious metals and wonder whether there might not also be a structural shift in the demand for CHF as safe haven currency. Developments in other asset classes such as Swiss real estate stocks are also cited as pointing in that direction. As we outlined in CHF: “Good as gold”, there are various factors that make investors consider CHF the “hard” asset in fiat FX. Rising concerns about geopolitics and debt sustainability could potentially accentuate these considerations and increase demand for CHF beyond the usual risk off periods – or at least trigger a persistent price adjustment. If such a shift was indeed occurring, the rate differential required to discourage inflows into CHF could be higher. We acknowledge this risk but see a few caveats. In addition, a disorderly depreciation is not in the interest of anyone, neither the US nor the rest of the world. If concerned about fiscal profligacy, look at real assets We have laid out our view as to why the narrative around persistent dollar weakness may be overblown in FX markets. However, that does not rule out a story about persistent loss of currency debasement, which is very far from being a US dollar prerogative. Fiscal profligacy is widespread, with a marked fiscal deterioration since the Global Financial Crisis (Exhibit 4). Furthermore, the lower-for-longer era is gone, and fiscal doves of the r<g type have had to switch the textbook. But if this is a fiscal story, we should be wondering about debasement, fiscal dominance, and whether the rally in real assets like gold still has room to run (Exhibit 4), rather than focusing on exchange rates. And if the main investor concerns are associated with geopolitics in addition to fiscal risks, gold would be a better hedge than other currencies. records.text: European Rates Weekly 30 January 2026 Citi Research 3 How much is the recent euro appreciation worth for HICP? Since the last projection round in December (cut-off, 10 working days to 26Nov25), EURUSD has appreciated around 3%, and the trade-weighted euro is up around 1% – Figure 1. Note that the cut-off for the March projections is probably around 20 February. It is primarily a dollar story, but it could still become more of a euro story over time should there be a growing trend of UST diversification and deeper European integration. As a rule-of-thumb, our European Economics team reckon a 10% change in trade-weighted euro has a 0.5%pt impact on the HICP level after 2 years. As they point out in the latest Euro Inflation Monitor, the ECB’s Chief Economist Phillip Lane believes the pass through could be a little higher. He has run models that suggest the impact on HICP could peak at 0.6%pts after 1 year before fading – see speech, 3Dec25. On that basis, the move in the trade-weighted euro so far might knock off around 0.06%pts from HICP in a year. Geopolitics and energy prices are the offset to FX. So far, the scale of euro appreciation, and its potential impact on HICP , is not enough to make a cut a live possibility. Moreover, there are offsetting drivers in the form of rallying commodity prices (of which energy is still by far the most important – see the Euro Inflation Monitor). Page 9 Foreign and Security Policy: While all parties share an emphasis on international cooperation in their foreign policy, their approaches and philosophies differ. The LDP, with the Japan-U.S. alliance as its cornerstone, leads the "Free and Open Indo- Pacific (FOIP)" initiative and seeks to maintain and expand Japan's influence in the international community by deepening ties with like-minded countries and the Global South. The CRA emphasizes dialogue and peaceful diplomacy, making clear its position of upholding an international order based on universal values such as freedom and democracy. The DPP also bases its policy on "dialogue, cooperation, and action," while particularly advocating for the promotion of "human rights diplomacy" and strengthening ties with the Global South to emphasize its contribution to the international community. In contrast, Sanseito prioritizes "Japan's national interest" and asserts that Japan should exercise independent leadership based on its history and culture, a stance characterized by its desire for a unique foreign policy not swayed by the trends of other nations. In defense policy, the parties are divided over the interpretation of traditional "exclusively defense-oriented policy."
