records.text: To estimate how the simulations might look, we construct a small macro model to approximate the BoE’s much larger structural model. In our model, the output gap is related to its own lag as well as current and expected interest rates, while inflation is related to its own lag as well as current and future output gaps. We also allow interest rates to affect inflation via exchange rate movements. We follow the BoE’s procedure for fitting the model to the central projection, which tells the model how inflation and the output gap will evolve if Bank Rate follows the market path. We then instead assume that policy is set in line with one of the Bank’s policy rules or assume that it follows an optimal policy path. One challenge is calibrating the model parameters. As a starting point, we take parameters from the BoE’s estimated structural model. This already generates a reasonable approximation of the policy paths when applied to the November 2025 forecast. But the fit is not perfect, for two reasons. First, our model is simpler than the Bank’s. Second, for this exercise the Bank used an (as yet unpublished) version of the model that adjusts the degree of forward-looking behaviour, which should affect the parameter estimates. As such, we tune the model to better fit the November 2025 paths for the policy rate, inflation, and the output gap across the Bank’s three different scenarios, implying modest changes to the parameters. But there are limits to how much real dollar depreciation can happen, not least because monetary policy abroad would react to it. Economics Focus Europe Date 29 January 2026 Testing the anchor: A deep dive into euro area inflation expectations This report assesses the stability of long -term inflation expectations in the euro area, a critical factor for the European Central Bank (ECB) as it navigates a period in which headline inflation will likely undershoot the 2% inflation target for a while. The ECB’s confidence in maintaining a steady policy stance hinges , in part, on the belief that these expectations are firmly anchored. Any de-anchoring could foster a disinflationary mindset among the public and prompt the central bank into policy easing to secure its credibility. To evaluate the strength of this anchor, our analysis utilizes a framework based on three core criteria suggested by NY Fed president John Williams: sensitivity of inflation expectations to economic shocks, consistency of inflation expectations with the 2% target ( level), and the behaviour of inflation uncertainty over the forecast horizon. records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 3 Returns differ: AI delivers durable productivity gains At the same time, AI investment offers a return profile distinct from property and traditional infrastructure. The marginal growth contribution from additional property investment is structurally low. To start with, roughly 30% of property investment consists of land purchases, which are excluded from capital formation in GDP accounting. Meanwhile, the return on each yuan of investment has declined sharply as the country builds up a large housing stock. AI capex, by contrast, involves minimal land cost: data centers are typically built on industrial land, which is substantially cheaper than residential land and often leased or subsidized by local governments. Beyond accounting, AI investment reinforces China’s position at the global technological frontier and delivers broad‑based productivity gains with a more durable long‑term return profile. A growing literature finds that AI‑related innovation has a disproportionately large impact on TFP— critical for sustaining potential growth as China’s labor force contracts. These productivity‑enhancing spillovers imply a more stable growth trajectory over time, even as the overall value of FAI steps down. Two waves of AI investment will reshape the FAI mix We expect AI‑related investment to unfold in two waves, with uneven effects on productivity across sectors. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 3 However, this assessment was based on the longer run forecasts in the December dot plot, which are premised on 2% inflation. Powell noted that core PCE inflation is likely to print at 3.0% y/y in December. Even if we exclude the tariff effect as a one-off, underlying inflation is above target. FOMC participants have argued that the tariffs have added 50-75bp to inflation. Our estimates are similar. Therefore, underlying inflation (ex of tariffs) is likely in the 2.25-2.5% range. And with fiscal policy turning notably easier this year, there is no clear impulse (other than lagged housing disinflation) for underlying inflation to move back to target. In turn, the real policy rate – which is what matters for the real economy – would be around 1.13-1.38%. This is close to, or lower than, six-to-nine participants’ implied longer run projections of the real rate (r*, i.e., their dot plot projections minus 2%). And it’s within touching distance of the longer run median real rate (1%). Another cut could push policy into accommodative territory, even based on the Fed’s somewhat conservative estimates of neutral (Exhibit 2). r* estimates are likely to keep getting marked up Powell also made other comments that suggested he is in the low neutral rate camp. In addition to dedicated oil capacity, a large share of gas-fired units can switch to oil during emergency periods. In total, up to 160 GW of generation capacity could theoretically rely on petroleum liquids, subject to regulatory waivers and fuel availability (Figure 13). US Department of Energy also authorized emergency measures allowing the use of additional oil-fired generation capacity despite air-quality or permit limitations, reinforcing the system’s ability to respond under stress. Gas-to-oil switching is activated regularly for generating electricity, as demonstrated by the oil consumption spikes (Figure 14). Gas-to-oil switching becomes especially attractive when a dollar’s worth of oil purchases more BTUs than gas, which has been the case this weekend, where brief intersections can be seen where oil becomes relatively cheaper to generate energy. Daily generation data show that oil-fired output increased by nearly 300 GWh/day versus pre-freeze levels of just 5–10 GWh/day. records.text: The other lever that is still in play is the composition of the Fed’s balance sheet. The prevailing thinking is either holding a “neutral portfolio” to match outstanding liabilities or a shorter duration portfolio. In either case, the Fed’s portfolio, at about 9+ years, is much longer than outstanding liabilities, at 6 years. Waller has been a big proponent of matching the Fed’s assets to its liabilities, which would reduce the risk of the Fed generating losses, as was the case in the past few years. Essentially this would mean backing reserves with T-bills, meaning the Fed is providing a liquidity transformation to banks rather than a maturity transformation. We suspect that Warsh would lend more support to this framework, meaning a shorter portfolio is more likely the landing spot for the long-run composition. There is no question the Fed needs to shorten its WAM in either framework; the question is the extent and how quickly it chooses to get there. We intend to watch closely how comments around both of these issues evolve in the coming months. 30 January 2026 3 Barclays | US Money Markets

Many moving parts: A detailed analysis of EA inflation and what has changed since the December projections shows a lot of moving parts: (i) December EA HICP likely came in lower than the ECB expected, which would imply negative base effects for the projection in 2026; (ii) oil and gas prices moved up recently, which would in principle move the ECB projections up. This is, however, partly offset by stronger eur/usd; and (iii) we (and market pricing) also failed to understand the strength of December ECB projections for 1Q26 (when commodity prices were expected to move further down). So, even with now higher energy prices, we would not rule out 1Q26 prints actually coming in lower than the ECB projected. The Governing Council will obviously have clearer visibility on these issues with the January flash EA HICP on 4 February, the day before the ECB meeting. But a couple more weeks to check whether the spike in natural gas prices and/or the euro appreciation persist would likely also be welcome, before a full update comes with the March projections (assumptions in March should have a cut-off date around 25 Feb). To summarise, this is a complex outlook, with many questions around the December projections. The Governing Council will likely simply acknowledge risks in both directions. However, subsequent news of the catalyst being pushed to 2026 reversed most of the price action. While the timing of the FOL limit increase remains uncertain, the recent announcement of an easing of Qualified Institutional Investor (QFI) restrictions starting on February 1, 2026 is a step in the direction for further market liberalization, with investors continuing to expect FOL increases later in the year, per our conversations. Our analysis suggests that an increase in the FOL limit to 100% could lead to Saudi Arabia’s weight in the MSCI EM rising by c.1pp from 2.9% to 3.7%, all else equal. How large would the impact on the economy and national finances (SNA basis, excluding regional finances) be if the consumption tax rate on food items (those currently subject to the reduced 8% rate) were lowered to 0%? The annual tax reduction would be JPY4.8trn, of which JPY3.7trn corresponds to the national tax portion. In addition, because 19.5% of consumption tax revenue is allocated to local allocation tax grants, the tax cut would reduce these grants by JPY0.7trn, resulting in a net JPY3trn deterioration in the primary balance (PB) as a direct national impact. Consumption tax cuts also affect GDP . By lowering tax‑inclusive prices, they are expected to shift consumption from the pre‑cut and post-cut periods into the tax‑cut period and stimulate spending by reducing the economic burden on households, thereby boosting real GDP . However, using multipliers from the Cabinet Office’s macroeconomic model (2022 edition), the decline in the GDP deflator caused by lower tax‑inclusive prices more than offsets the increase in real GDP , lowering nominal GDP . Moreover, because food is a necessity with low price elasticity, the real GDP-boosting effect would likely be more limited than for a broad‑based tax cut. records.text: 4 US Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 A different kind of overheating The Fed will likely be inertial in coming around to a higher neutral rate. Particularly under the next Chair, who is likely to lean into a low neutral rate view (similar to Governor Miran), as a way of justifying their (expected) dovish leaning. This creates risk of overheating later this year and into 2027. Our above-consensus inflation forecast of 2.8% y/y core PCE at year-end is premised on i) an economy that is running hot due to fiscal and monetary easing, and ii) additional tariff pass-through in coming months. One reason we aren’t expecting a much bigger inflation wave from policy easing is the K-shaped nature of consumer spending. Asset-rich higher-income households are already seeing strong spending growth. Therefore, their marginal propensity to spend any additional income/wealth could be somewhat low at this stage: instead, they might invest in financial markets. Our conclusion is that if if the Fed ends up over-easing, the impact could be felt more in asset inflation than price inflation.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Inflation Attitudes Survey, high inflation in the UK, on average, leads consumers to either cut back spending and save more, or shop around for better-value goods and services. It is also possible to argue, as Chief Economist Pill has intimated in his 2025 speeches, that de-anchored inflation expectations might translate to a surge in pay demands should the labour market eventually retighten. This year, however, UK pay growth decelerated precipitously (from 5.9% 3M/Y in January, on the ex-bonus measure in the private sector, to 3.6% 3M/Y in November). Virtually all surveys suggest further pay disinflation, albeit to differing degrees. With 2.5 job-seekers for each vacancy, we struggle to see a tight labour market any time soon. In any case, we think that inflation expectations are almost certainly due to fall further in the March iteration of the Ipsos survey. Historically, inflation expectations react to a peak in headline inflation with a two-quarter lag. While we had been worried about a structural break in inflation expectations among the older age cohorts – akin to that notable in the GfK's consumer confidence survey following the July 2024 elections – we find little evidence of this in the disaggregated Ipsos data. We believe that inflation expectations will fall this year, as they have fallen in 2024, in sympathy with spot inflation. In practice, one needs to choose between predominantly matching the vega and getting "close enough" on the gamma (through an intermediate expiry swaption like 3y10y), or predominantly matching the short gamma exposure, but not recreating the short vega exposure. As rate vol market observers for a long period of time, our view is that the latter is generally a more profitable method to be short vol (more below), although it is much more intensive in terms of implementation. We describe it below. Replicate only short gamma through an equivalent portfolio of short expiry swaptions In this method, one ignores the sensitivity of MBS to implied volatility and focuses on replacing the carry arising through short convexity by selling some short expiry swaptions at a liquid point on the vol surface such as 3m10y. If rates do not move, the short option position decays positively. If rates move higher, the delta of the short option position together with the duration exposure of the cash Treasury leg replicates the extension risk of the MBS. records.text: 6 Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 A different kind of overheating The Fed will likely be inertial in coming around to a higher neutral rate. Particularly under the next Chair, who is likely to lean into a low neutral rate view (similar to Governor Miran), as a way of justifying their (expected) dovish leaning. This creates risk of overheating later this year and into 2027. Our above-consensus inflation forecast of 2.8% y/y core PCE at year-end is premised on i) an economy that is running hot due to fiscal and monetary easing, and ii) additional tariff pass-through in coming months. One reason we aren’t expecting a much bigger inflation wave from policy easing is the K-shaped nature of consumer spending. Asset-rich higher-income households are already seeing strong spending growth. Therefore, their marginal propensity to spend any additional income/wealth could be somewhat low at this stage: instead they might invest in financial markets. Our conclusion is that if the Fed ends up over-easing, the impact could be felt more in asset inflation than price inflation. .

Moreover, we continue to recommend 10y iota tighteners, having moved up our stop to lock in at least modest gains. Front-end opportunity In terms of the very front end, we find arguments to go long 1y BEs compelling, basically creating a barbell approach to our long breakeven expression. The thinking is basically that: • 1y BEs have actually underperformed in January (after adjusting for carry and RBOB, Figure• 2) • From a fundamental basis, the market-implied core fixing path looks quite sanguine at• basically 0.15-0.20% m/m from March through November (Figures 10 and 11 of our Inflation- Linked Daily) • The TIIJan27s are both slightly cheap to Barclays forecast (whereas they arguably should be• trading slightly rich given expectations of above-trend growth justifying a modest positive inflation risk premium) ( Figure 4) • The tenor faced a notable headwind this month due to the weakest January carry profile in• several years ( more on that below).

records.text: United States: Money Markets Déjà vu all over again? The Treasury is (again) exploring issuing a SOFR-indexed FRN, which would add another avenue for issuance as it leans more on the very front-end. With risks of a government shutdown (again) looming over IRS operations, we look at potential effects on the TGA as tax season begins. Funding markets continue to trade in a very benign fashion this week with SOFR being well behaved, printing within a few basis points of IORB even as net Treasury T-bill settlements have turned positive, and GSE cash has exited after the end of their float period ( Figure 1). We have been calling for smooth funding markets in Q1 amid Fed balance sheet expansion and a rebound in balance sheet capacity at US GSIBs, and that continues to be our expectation for the months ahead. The Fed was the event of the week, but left funding markets with nothing new on balance sheet after the fireworks of last year. We were hoping for a few details around its thinking over how to structure RMPs in the longer run, to help gauge risks of how much it might dial back the level of purchases after tax season effects on the TGA have faded. But the balance sheet was absent from the post-meeting press conference, and that leaves us looking to the meeting minutes in three week's time for the tenor of discussions on the topic. records.text: US Rates Weekly 30 January 2026 Citi Research 14 Vol: Warsh Fed is positive for curve vol We believe a Warsh-led Fed should bias the curve steeper and help curve vol outperform rates vol with front-end and long-end rates staying more decorrelated than usual. We recommend buying 6m curve cap on 2s30s and selling 6m7y swaption straddle for positive carry and steepening bias. Curve volatility picking up despite stagnant rates Outright moves in rates remain muted, and the FOMC’s rate pause this week, along with the affirmation of a gradual meeting-by-meeting approach, means that rates will likely stay range-bound in the near-term. However, despite this doldrum backdrop, realized volatility on the broader 2s30s curve has started to pick up recently and even slightly exceeded the realized volatility on belly rates, which is a rare occurrence (Figure 24). The outperformance in curve vol relative to rates vol is primarily due to the recent twisting of the curve where front-end and long-end rates have been more decorrelated than usually and even occasionally moved in opposite directions. The ratio of belly rate realized vol vs curve realized vol has fallen to its multi-year low, which is consistent with the extreme realized decorrelation between the 2y and 30y rates (Figure 25). Going forward, we believe that front-end and long-end rates can stay more decorrelated than usual, especially with Kevin Warsh as the newly nominated Fed Chair. China’s property downturn is now in its fifth year, while AI‑related FAI continues to accelerate on policy support and intensifying US–China tech competition. For now, AI‑related FAI is far smaller than the hole left by real estate, underscoring the need for counter-cyclical policy support in services-sector FAI this year. That said, AI investment is likely to narrow the gap with property by 2027–28 and offers durable TFP gains, particularly in knowledge‑intensive sectors where productivity spillovers can be significant. As these dynamics unfold, the composition of FAI is likely to shift further toward services, with AI deployment becoming increasingly important after the initial IT‑ and power‑capex‑heavy first wave of investment. This is the third instalment of our Unravelling China’s Investment series (See previous reports at: The Factory Woes and The Infrastructure Slump). Week ahead In the coming week, we turn our focus to the monetary policy meetings in India and Australia, along with data release in Korea. In India, we expect the RBI to cut the policy rate by 25bp to 5.00% and announce more liquidity measures in the Feb meeting. Current price action is starting to seem divorced from fundamentals, in our view, raising the risk of an interim correction. The gold:silver ratio has dropped materially, highlighting how the diversification interest is spreading rapidly to the rest of the precious metals space, as investors move into hard assets and put on catch-up trades. There is also likely an increasing amount of short- term speculative interest, which creates more volatility. We are cautious about chasing the market higher at this point, especially for those looking to put on fresh positions. So, while the forceful rally in gold and precious metals more broadly indicates there is plenty of FOMO (fear of missing out) around, we think sometimes it is also healthy to acknowledge JOMO (joy of missing out) and be patient in picking entry levels. There is of course the risk that waiting too long for deep-enough corrections that never come only serves to amplify the upside when everyone jumps in at the same time so as not to miss the move even further. This has been the general experience for most of this bull cycle. The difference this time around, in our view, is that the spillover into the rest of precious metals has been much more pronounced than it has been in the past, suggesting that there is more froth in the market. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 30 January 2026 13 Returns differ: AI delivers durable productivity gains At the same time, AI investment offers a return profile distinct from property and traditional infrastructure. The marginal growth contribution from additional property investment is structurally low. To start with, roughly 30% of property investment consists of land purchases, which are excluded from capital formation in GDP accounting. Meanwhile, the return on each yuan of investment has declined sharply as the country builds up a large housing stock. AI capex, by contrast, involves minimal land cost: data centers are typically built on industrial land, which is substantially cheaper than residential land and often leased or subsidized by local governments. Beyond accounting, AI investment reinforces China’s position at the global technological frontier and delivers broad‑based productivity gains with a more durable long‑term return profile. A growing literature finds that AI‑related innovation has a disproportionately large impact on TFP— critical for sustaining potential growth as China’s labor force contracts. These productivity‑enhancing spillovers imply a more stable growth trajectory over time, even as the overall value of FAI steps down. Two waves of AI investment will reshape the FAI mix We expect AI‑related investment to unfold in two waves, with uneven effects on productivity across sectors. records.text: 30 January 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG A status-check: The preliminary 2025 federal budget results in review In this note, we take a close look at the preliminary annual results for the 2025 federal budget, explain why the federal spending and deficit targets were missed, and how these should be classified with regard to our 2026 general government (national accounts) deficit forecast. The analysis builds on our previous work regarding Germany's fiscal policy shift (see also here and here). The data is based on the January 2026 Monthly Report of the Federal Ministry of Finance, which contains the preliminary annual results of the federal core budget and the latest December 2025 credit borrowing flows for the off-budgetary units for the Federal Armed Forces (SV BW) and the newly established Infrastructure & Climate Protection Fund (SV IK). Federal government significantly missed its spending and deficit targets As we anticipated, the federal government deficit turned out to be significantly lower than planned, according to financial statistics data (cash flow perspective). Specifically, the 2025 financial deficit in the regular core budget reached "only" EUR 65 bn (compared to a target of EUR 82 bn). Meanwhile, the financing deficits for the SV BW and SV IK reached "only" EUR 20 bn and EUR 24 bn, respectively, thus also falling short of their targets of EUR 24 bn and EUR 37 bn. records.text: Marija Veitmane 30 January 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Earnings beats are not always enough Three weeks into the final quarter of 2025 earnings season, the market has been left somewhat disappointed. While more than 80% of U.S. companies have beaten analysts’ expectations (70% globally), the median surprise is below average and share prices have more often declined on reporting day. We believe this disappointment stems largely from two factors: expectations were already set low, making many beats feel insufficient—especially when paired with soft forward guidance, leading to sharp punishment for misses — and little signs of earnings growth broadening beyond the crowded Tech trade. We are mostly disappointed by the limited progress toward earnings broadening. The vast majority of earnings continue to come from the IT sector, while two sectors—Energy and Consumer Discretionary—remain on track for outright earnings contraction, and two others—Consumer Staples and Real Estate—are growing earnings at a pace below inflation. Industrials delivered strong reported results, adding roughly 3% to full‑year 2025 earnings growth, but much of this strength reflects surging demand for power‑generation equipment from data centres—another extension of the AI trade rather than true sector‑wide improvement. Banks continue to post solid beats driven by capital markets activity, yet the lack of meaningful lending growth has kept analysts from raising forward expectations.

The dollar may have lost some of its luster, including its hedging properties. But there are limits to how much real dollar depreciation can happen, not least because monetary policy abroad would react to it. And if the story is about fiscal profligacy and currency debasement, we should be asking how much more room to run real assets may have. United States: Is policy already accommodative? In the Jan press conference, Powell suggested that most of the FOMC still thinks rates are restrictive. But the real policy rate looks to be very close to the Fed’s r* estimate. Moreover, the Fed appears to be underestimating potential growth (and therefore r*). Policy might already be accommodative. We see risks of overheating due to easy fiscal and monetary policy in coming months. But in a K-shaped economy, that might be reflected in financial asset inflation rather than price inflation. records.text: ederal Statistical Office, Deutsche Bank Research Taken all together, the combined deficit concluded at "just" around EUR 110 bn (roughly 2.5% of GDP). Consequently, the 2025 outcome was more than EUR 30 bn lower than the federal government's target of EUR 143 bn (3.2% of GDP). At the regular core budget (still where most federal spendin g occurs), the improved budget balance was equally driven by stronger-than-expected revenues (EUR 7 bn) and lower-than-targeted expenditures (EUR 9 bn) (see figure 4). On the revenue side, other revenues in particular significantly exceeded expectations, coming in more than EUR 5 bn higher than estimated. Even tax revenues, despite Germany's persistently weak economic growth, were almost EUR 2 bn above the target. Although the federal deficit and spending targets were significantly undershot, the fiscal regime shift is becoming increasingly visible in the financial statistics data: Measured against the 2024 baseline – the starting point before the initiation of the fiscal policy shift – the combined deficit more than doubled (2024 actual: EUR 42 bn or 1% of GDP). Moreover, the aggregated expenditures of the core budget as well as the SV BW and SV IK rose by more than 10% over the past year (see figure 1 and 17). In addition, AI may disrupt the labor market, as task automation tends to reduce labor’s share of income and increase capital’s share, especially where AI substitutes for human tasks at scale 2. Regulation, reform, and more flexible labor allocation In our view, the boost to potential growth will depend on how effectively workers displaced or redeployed by AI are matched to productive roles and sectors. In China’s case, well‑known hurdles to labor mobility and reallocation could limit how fully the economy captures productivity gains during this transition. More efficient reallocation will channel resources to higher‑productivity locations and sectors, and support GDP growth. Next week brings the Treasury quarterly refunding meeting, and we expect the Treasury to reaffirm its guidance that it plans to maintain nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes "for at least the next several quarters. " We see no need for any changes to this guidance, given our expectation of no auction size increases in 2026 (see here). That would leave a funding gap of about $700bn between the expected deficit and net coupon issuance, which Treasury would need to fill through T-bill issuance. We expect the Fed to buy about $500bn of this gap as it grows reserves and replaces MBS on its balance sheet. That would leave net issuance to private investors of just $200bn this year, which looks quite manageable, but that gap would grow notably in 2027 if coupon auction sizes remain unchanged. This likely has Treasury thinking about its issuance mix for next year and as part of its dealer discussions, the Treasury asked for feedback about SOFR-indexed floating-rate note issuance, likely as it assesses demand levels if it were to introduce this as a new product. The Treasury has asked about SOFR floater issuance in the past, suggesting some leg work has already been done. In 2020, it requested public comments on the possibility of issuing such a note. In the US, although Comex silver inventories have been falling, levels are still higher than they were before the tariff uncertainty started to trigger global movements of metal in late 2024/early 2025. Silver held in London vaults has been recovering since September last year, though overall levels still look low relative to historical average of over 1.1 moz. Silver 1m forward swap rates have eased and shorter tenors more generally are back in contango. Longer dates, however, remain in backwardation. Investors' interest in silver has surged along with prices and price volatility. Tightening market conditions underpin prices, but are unlikely to be solely responsible for price action. We think there is still enough silver around, but sometimes not in the right form or location and it can take a while to move.

As an extreme example of the difference between systematically being short vega and systematically being short gamma, consider Figure 9, which compares the performance of being short 3y10y swaptions on a delta hedged/ rolling basis (we simulate selling $10mn notional of 3y10y swaptions every day, hold them for three months and then roll) vs being short 1m10y swaptions on a delta hedged/rolling basis (we simulate selling 10mm of 1m10y swaptions every day, delta hedged to expiry). We have ignored transaction costs here, but the main point is that over the long term, systematic short exposure to 3y10y tends to lose, while systematic short exposure to short expiry options tends to be rather profitable. Only during very low vol environments such as 2015 to 2019 do both strategies work similarly. This is, in fact, why systematic long vega is an actively traded strategy in rates vol (even though those long vol strategies typically use much longer expiries like 10y10y), and so is short-gamma/long vega through calendar spreads. The underperformance from being short rate vega rather than short gamma can matter when the objective is to generate out-performance. We think that market participants are generally aware that selling intermediate expiry rate vol such as 3y10y tends to be a poorly performing trade over the long run. Powell noted that core PCE inflation is likely to print at 3.0% y/y in December. Even if we exclude the tariff effect as a one-off, underlying inflation is above target. FOMC participants have argued that the tariffs have added 50-75bp to inflation. Our estimates are similar. Therefore, underlying inflation (ex of tariffs) is likely in the 2.25-2.5% range. And with fiscal policy turning notably easier this year, there is no clear impulse (other than lagged housing disinflation) for underlying inflation to move back to target. In turn, the real policy rate – which is what matters for the real economy – would be around 1.13-1.38%. This is close to, or lower than, six-to-nine participants’ implied longer run projections of the real rate (r*, i.e., their dot plot projections minus 2%). And it’s within touching distance of the longer run median real rate (1%). records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 28 November) Real GDP contracted in Q3 for the first negative growth in six quarters, reflecting a sharp drop in housing investment and sluggish exports linked to tariffs. However, as the former was driven by institutional factors, we expect a return to positive growth from Q4. Looking ahead, we expect growth of around 1% on average due primarily to firm capital investment on the back of structural factors such as labor-saving expenditures and stable consumption stemming from a recovery in the real income environment under slowing inflation. Although the economic measures decided by the Takaichi administration are limited in terms of their growth-boosting effect relative to scale, they are likely to provide a certain degree of support to the economy. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. Furthermore, services inflation has become increasingly robust as the dynamic synergy between wages and prices strengthens on the back of irreversible structural changes in the labor market. History suggests upside into the MSCI announcement, but not durable gains While the market reaction to the FOL news in September provides a template, we look back at prior episodes of FOL increases across emerging markets to assess whether these changes drive durable upside for the respective market, and to gauge how investors typically position into these announcements. Over the past 10 years, notable FOL increases were announced and implemented by Saudi Arabia (to facilitate entry into the MSCI EM index), China, India, Kuwait (MSCI EM upgrade), UAE and Qatar. We acknowledge that each of these events is nuanced, with differences around actual implementation. For example, Saudi Arabia’s foreign ownership limit changes paved the way for the market to be included in the MSCI EM index, which was implemented in 2 phases. Similarly, the increase in China’s weight in the MSCI EM index in 2019 was effected in 3 phases. Separately, the 2021 foreign ownership limit increases in both UAE and Qatar represent regulatory decisions — with the changes to index weights occurring via individual company approvals later on. In contrast, investment in knowledge‑intensive sectors such as IT and finance was more resilient. But US tariff threats to Canada and South Korea are noteworthy, still. Remember the EU has yet to ratify the US-EU trade deal from last year, and to extend the suspension of counter-tariffs on US goods by 7 Feb – the ball is in the court of the EU parliament on both counts into next week. We don’t expect escalation from the EU, but it is worth keeping an eye on the discussion. Meanwhile, the EU-India trade deal agreed last week is good news. Ratification could be long and bumpy (think Mercusor). First-round income gains are probably not a game- changer per se (Kiel Institute estimates are for 12-13bp p.a.), but bigger gains can come from more dynamic activity later on. What dominates is the symbol, we think. We argued a few months back, Europe is “being pushed” into building stronger relationships with the rest of the world as the US withdraws. records.text: lizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 50k in 2026 after coming in at 15k in 2H25. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate ticking up to just 4.5% in 4Q25, where it should remain in 1H26 before dropping to 4.3% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5-3.75% at the January meeting, as expected. In the characterization of current conditions, the Fed leaned into the Dec u-rate decline. Powell’s comments on the labor market mirrored the optimism in the statement. But he also highlighted some pockets of concern. We remain comfortable with our view that the Fed won’t cut again under Powell. We have penciled in two 25bp cuts under the next Chair, with low conviction, in June and July. Policy under the next Chair will depend a lot on the composition of the FOMC. This leaves our projection of the terminal rate unchanged at 3.0-3.25%.

records.text: T-bills. The Fed has limited control over many of these larger items, two of which are the TGA and currency in circulation. The TGA, which is Treasury’s cash balance at the Fed, is set such that Treasury holds enough cash to fund itself for seven calendar days, assuming a loss of market access. That currently has it targeting a quarter-end balance of $850bn. Currency in circulation has historically grown faster than the broader nominal economy. As banks and households demand for currency rises, the Fed issues more cash, and currently that total is about $2.4tn. That means the Fed needs over $3tn in securities alone before it even creates $1 of bank reserves. Those measures are temporary tax incentives established separately from the tax code to achieve specific policy aims. The MoF estimates that those measures reduced tax revenues by some ¥9.5trn in FY23. Existing special tax measures include corporate tax cuts to promote R&D and support small businesses; income tax breaks such as home mortgage tax relief; and gasoline tax cuts and naphtha tax exemptions to protect and nurture specific industries. We believe that the effectiveness of these special measures needs to be studied carefully, especially those related to corporate taxes, which are varied in type and extremely complex. That would hopefully lead to a fairer and simpler tax system. records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 29 January 2026 Citi Research 3 Intervention risk has risen across the board. Last week, we cut our long standing JGB underweight in GAA, largely because Japanese rates accelerated higher in an unsustainable manner, particularly the super long end sector, raising the likelihood of intervention. Back then, there were three distinct ‘intervention’ worries. First, the BOJ could become more hawkish in their policy meeting. Second, the MoF could intervene in the JGB market, or it could intervene in the FX market. In the event, the BOJ did not become meaningfully more hawkish in its January policy meeting, though this may well have been driven by a desire to remain quiet ahead of the snap election on Feb 8th. Things may change post-election. On JGBs, Finance Minister Katayama urged calm in the JGB market, but did not directly suggest intervention. With respect to FX, we came closest to intervention, as the Fed checked USDJPY rates with dealers, generating a large JPY rally (BBG, 26 Jan). FX intervention plausible, but likely after election. While the rate check by the Federal Reserve suggests that currency intervention is a clear possibility, it appears that such an intervention would be unilateral, (where the Fed would act as an agent for the Japanese MoF). Bernanke (2022) estimates that QE supplemented by lower-for-longer forward guidance can provide the equivalent for up to 3 additional percentage points of policy space. Smaller balance sheet means steeper curves and higher term premium The precise impact on growth and inflation of any balance sheet reduction may be difficult to measure, but a reduction in UST holdings by the Fed would imply higher holdings of US Treasuries for more price sensitive investors. Hedge funds and foreigners have increased their share of US Treasuries as the Federal Reserve started its QT back in 2022 (see Figure 3). Waiting for clarity Discussions with clients suggest that focus has shifted from uncertainty around the extent of the easing cycle to some uncertainty around the balance sheet run-off. Senate confirmation hearings may provide more clarity on this, also on how the new Chair would see the role of financial regulations in setting the size of the balance sheet . Till more clarity appears, investors could demand higher excess returns (term premium) to hold long-dated bonds. Ultimately though, we think the Fed will shy away from a sharp change away from the status quo on the balance sheet and that Trump 2.0 is still a carry and risk-positive environment. If at some point the Federal Reserve decides to take a more hawkish view on the outlook, then it's quite likely that USD would benefit as investors turn their attention back towards data. So, investors should be mindful of volatility in both directions, with drivers of USD oscillating between conventional and unconventional drivers, which likely means that the correlation of USD and US equities is more inconsistent and unreliable. In our view, this suggests that investors should continue to consider hedging the FX exposure of their USD assets. This is a relevant consideration for investors not just in Europe but also in other regions. To be clear, we are not suggesting that investors will diversify their asset holdings. Importantly, striking a neutral tone not only preserves maximum optionality, but also reflects the internal balance of views within the GC, where opinions on the inflation outlook and related risks remain divided. Until the March forecast round, we expect the ECB to focus on a series of elements: whether the investment outlook continues to improve; signals from the wages-services nexus; the impact of China's overcapacity on both activity and prices; and EUR appreciation. The first three are relatively slow-moving and afford the GC time to analyse and react, whereas further EUR strength could raise the GC's policy sensitivity. In addition, the effect of annual price resets in January and February will warrant close monitoring. With inflation now largely normalised, we expect price resets in many slow-moving services categories to generate a drag of around 0.1pp on services inflation in January. Last year, ECB Vice-President de Guindos said EUR gains beyond $1.20 would become "complicated" . More recently, while describing the euro's gains as "modest" , Austrian Governor Kocher told the Financial Times that "if the euro appreciates further and further, at some stage this might create of course a certain necessity to react in terms of monetary policy" . That is because the incoming data have been broadly in line with the staff’s projections, there has been no significant shift in the economic outlook, and ECB officials continue to see the current policy stance as appropriate. President Lagarde is therefore likely to reiterate that policy is in a “good place” for the sixth consecutive meeting. Looking ahead, our growth and inflation forecasts are similar to the staff n projections, and we agree with the Council’s assessment that monetary policy can stay on hold for the time being. The more interesting question relates to the hurdle for action, and our recent work suggests it would take a material change in the economic outlook for the Council to move policy from here. We upgrade our price forecasts and earnings, forecast a 2026 year- end gold price of $5,600/oz and lift our gold price estimates +11-12% over 2026-27E to $5,200/$4,800oz. While gold feels a 'consensus long' trade and we remain cognisant that no bull market lasts forever, in our view the macro logic for gold remains robust and we do not see the set-up for a bear market in 2026. We see the logic for sustained buying from Central Banks (despite higher prices) and whilst most gold models are currently 'broken', the 5 gold bear markets in the last ~50yrs occurred during periods of: (1) increasing economic growth; (2) reducing inflation/expectations; (3) stronger USD; (4) reduced risk premia/uncertainty. We expect the opposite of these variables over the next 6-12mth and believe this combined with ongoing de-dollarisation/debasement trade will sustain asset allocations to gold. On the miners, we see strong balance sheets (mostly net cash), with growing cash positions, as miners look to organic growth options that look increasingly accretive given where prices are now. France's Governor Villeroy de Galhau said the ECB is monitoring the EUR's appreciation and its possible consequences for inflation, highlighting that it will be one of the factors guiding interest-rate decisions over the coming months. That said, not all GC members would endorse a heightened sensitivity to the exchange rate: Governor Šimkus cautioned that it is an oversimplification to argue for policy adjustment simply because the EUR has strengthened to current levels. For this debate to gain traction at the March meeting, we would need to see further EUR appreciation and evidence that the FX move is persistent. That would strengthen the case that the undershoot is both deeper and more prolonged than currently projected. Our base case continues to foresee the ECB maintaining the deposit rate at 2% throughout 2026–27. However, we judge that risks are tilted towards calibrating policy rates lower, with the deposit rate potentially moving to 1.5% to lean against an extended period of inflation undershooting. This likely explains the recent toning‑down of the tax cut rhetoric. January Tokyo CPI inflation: BoJ core continues to slow In the January CPI data for Tokyo, inflation excluding perishables and energy (aka "BoJ core") came to +2.4% y/y (December: +2.6%), easing for a second consecutive month and undershooting market expectations ( Figure 10, Figure 11). This was due to a smaller contribution primarily from food ex-perishables, but also from hotel charges, likely driven by the steep drop in Chinese visitors to Japan. Month on month, the index was flat (+0.1%), slowing from the previous month. CPI inflation excluding perishables alone ("core") eased more significantly y/y, slowing to +2.0% (December: +2.3%), as did overall inflation, to +1.5% (+2.0%). These readings were also below market consensus and due primarily to a decline in the provisional tax rate on gasoline. Although the latest readings missed expectations, they were consistent with our view that BoJ core inflation, which is not directly affected by the government's energy policies, is already in a trend of gradual deceleration (see below). We maintain our call for further BoJ rate hikes in July and December. 30 January 2026 12 Ba

ECB President Lagarde will likely be quizzed on the rise in energy prices and the EUR. We doubt she will engage much in the discussion and emphasise instead the rise in uncertainty. At the margin, that could make for a slightly dovish read; even if it is a reiteration of the December message. We still expect the ECB to cut in March, but as we flagged last week, our conviction is fading. German inflation specifically and recent energy price moves more broadly are still compatible with downward surprises to the ECB’s 1.9% inflation forecast for 1Q26, but the scope of downside looks a little smaller than we initially thought. Absent major surprises in national prints, we expect Euro area HICP at 1.7%yoy headline and 2.2% core in next week’s January print. Our conviction of an overall easing bias is unbroken though. Underlying disinflation is on track in December, as our seasonally adjusted bottom-up inflation metrics show (European Disinflation Tracker: encouraging Dec data). Energy prices and EUR strength are a mix to reduce medium-term inflation. And uncertainty is not good for growth. The economy is improving, or at least so we hope The easing bias is not incompatible with improving growth. Interest has picked up across the board and any signs of opportunistic profit-taking from long-term holders have been more than offset by the surge in renewed interest. The continued inflows into gold ETFs reflects the persistence of institutional as well as retail interest. Gold ETFs trading in China and the US in particular have seen strong inflows so far this year. Fresh investor allocations that typically get put on at the start of the year have likely accelerated given the macro and geopolitical developments so far this year. Although circumstances remain fluid, we think the unprecedented levels of uncertainty, unpredictability and unknown unknowns that investors face in the year ahead suggest that core allocations to gold are likely to be more durable and not easily fazed by any easing in any one of these factors. The bar is high, many things will have to be resolved all at once, and/or traditional macro drivers will have to turn significantly negative towards gold for market participants to fully abandon positions or flip to a net short. Physical demand has been strong, and while this is in line with historical seasonal patterns, it is nevertheless surprising in the context of the rapid rise in prices to new record levels. The BoE's published estimates peg the neutral rate at between 2% and 4%, with the mid-point of 3%, broadly in line with the figure endorsed by external member Taylor and Deputy Governor Ramsden. External member Greene and Deputy Governor Lombardelli highlight that they are unsure whether the BoE is restrictive. To us, the sluggish state of the UK's most rate-sensitive sectors (construction and housing), as well as the 1pp rise in the jobless rate over the past year, strongly suggest that the BoE is still quite restrictive. Monetary policy, after all, works in the output gap space – not only in the demand one. In any case, in the absence of a fast-paced deterioration in the growth data – where risks of a such a non-linear outcome did look negligible back in November and December, but have been lessened following the January PMIs and the November GDP print – the evolution of the spot nominal data will probably have to change priors around the neutral rate. That reluc- tance still lingers, judging by real yields. This argues for patience and we look for a tactical opportunity post-meeting to enter front- end flattening trades. The natural expression is AUD 1s/2s IRS: if we are right that neutral is in the lower 3s, subsequent easing should be priced in the forwards. Front-end valuation models suggest 1Yx1Y is relatively cheaper than 1Y (Figure 7A U D 1 Y x 1 Y i s c h e a p t o t h e R B A H D S , i n f l a t i o n a n d u n e m p l o y m e n t , a n d w h i l e m o d e l s m a y b e b i a s e d b y p r e v i o u s c y c l e s , t h i s s h o u l d w a s h o u t t o s o m e e x t e n t i n t h e r e l a t i v e r e s i d u a l s b e t w e e n 1 Y a n d 1 Y x 1 Y ), and similarly that 1s/2s is too steep (Figure 8T h e 1 s / 2 s A U D s w a p c u r v e s p r e a d i s s i m i l a r l y s t e e p t o f u n d a m e n t a l s ), controlling for 3m OIS, RBA and Fed HDSs, Australian unemployment and inflation. The RBA Hawk Dove Score is a key input to these models, and independent of the choice taken next week would expect the HDS to move up, potentially boosting fair value. This is another reason to exercise patience given the unusual circumstances surround- ing the meeting.
